evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends standard developmental intervention, of which speech and language therapy is a component.

treatments/2.description: Because most affected individuals are nonverbal or minimally verbal, speech and language therapy focused on augmentative and alternative communication is a core, lifelong intervention rather than an optional adjunct.

evidence.snippet: improvement trends in feeding, hypotonia, verbalisation, and motor skills over time
evidence.explanation: Documented improvement in hypotonia and motor skills supports an active rehabilitative approach.

treatments/3.description: Physiotherapy for hypotonia, motor delay, joint laxity and contracture prevention, with durable medical equipment and orthotics as needed. Longitudinal data show motor skills improve over time, so rehabilitation goals should be progressive rather than purely maintenance.

evidence.snippet: We targeted self-injury in a child with BRPS using a functional analysis and differential reinforcement, with several extensions to common procedures. Results present the first example of behavioral reduction for self-injury in BRPS.
evidence.explanation: The first published behavioural treatment demonstration in this disorder, supporting the approach while acknowledging n=1.

evidence.snippet: There are no published treatments for BRPS.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the absence of an established treatment evidence base at the time of publication, contextualizing the weight of this single case.

treatments/4.description: Structured behaviour-analytic assessment and treatment, using functional analysis and differential reinforcement, is the best-evidenced non-pharmacological approach to self-injury in this disorder. Coexisting sleep disruption can confound assessment and should be addressed in parallel.

evidence.snippet: The introduction of Pregabalin leads to rapid stabilization of the clinical state, almost complete improvement in challenging behavior and gradual withdrawal of other treatments (class 2 analgesics, neuroleptics, antidepressants, and benzodiazepines).
evidence.explanation: Supports the observation in a single patient. Marked PARTIAL because an uncontrolled n=1 report cannot establish efficacy.

treatments/5.description: Reported in a single adult with BRPS, severe intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy admitted for severe self- and hetero-aggression, in whom pregabalin produced rapid stabilization and allowed withdrawal of analgesics, neuroleptics, antidepressants and benzodiazepines, sustained at nine months. This is hypothesis-generating only.

evidence.snippet: standard treatment for epilepsy, joint contractures, sleep apnea, dental anomalies, strabismus and/or refractive error
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends standard epilepsy treatment; no disorder-specific regimen is specified.

evidence.snippet: Bainbridge-Ropers syndrome is associated with childhood-onset generalized epilepsy with generalized tonic-clonic seizures and/or atypical absence seizures.
evidence.explanation: Defines the epilepsy syndrome that anti-seizure medication choice should target.

treatments/6.description: Standard neurologist-directed management of childhood-onset generalized epilepsy with generalized tonic-clonic and atypical absence seizures. Broad-spectrum agents are the rational choice given the generalized phenotype, but there are no BRPS-specific efficacy data. Confirm that paroxysmal events are epileptic on video-EEG before escalating, since breath-holding, hyperventilation and dystonic episodes in this disorder are non-epileptic.

evidence.snippet: Dental evaluation every six months after age three years or as clinically indicated.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews surveillance recommendation for dental care.

treatments/7.description: Six-monthly dental review from age three, with preventive measures. Dental anomalies are a recognized feature and oral health is difficult to maintain in a nonverbal child with behavioural challenges.

evidence.snippet: At least annual ophthalmology evaluation.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews ophthalmological surveillance recommendation.

evidence.snippet: Our recommendations include: baseline renal imaging after diagnosis, and Dental and Ophthalmological follow-up for all.
evidence.explanation: Adds baseline renal imaging to the surveillance plan on the basis of a newly recognized renal phenotype.

treatments/8.description: At least annual ophthalmology review for all, given the frequency of strabismus and refractive error. Baseline renal imaging after diagnosis is a newer recommendation arising from the emerging renal phenotype identified in the international natural history study.

evidence.snippet: If the ASXL3 pathogenic variant identified in the proband is not identified in either parent, the risk to sibs is presumed to be low but greater than that of the general population because of the possibility of parental germline mosaicism.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews recurrence-risk statement that counseling must convey.

evidence.snippet: Once the ASXL3 pathogenic variant has been identified in an affected family member, prenatal testing for a pregnancy at increased risk and preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the reproductive options to be discussed.

evidence.snippet: We documented recurrence in nontwin siblings due to parental mosaicism.
evidence.explanation: Provides the concrete observed basis for the mosaicism recurrence-risk counselling point.

treatments/9.description: Counseling should cover the autosomal dominant, usually de novo, mode of inheritance; the low but non-zero sibling recurrence risk from parental germline or gonosomal mosaicism; the availability of prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing once a familial variant is known; and the option of ultra-deep parental sequencing to refine recurrence risk after an apparently de novo diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: ASXL3 mRNA transcripts from the mutated allele are prone to nonsense-mediated decay, and expression of ASXL3 is reduced.
evidence.explanation: Patient-cell measurement of reduced ASXL3 expression, the direct support for a dosage mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Therefore we emphasize that BRPS syndrome, caused by ASXL3 loss-of-function variants, is a clinically distinct intellectual disability syndrome with a recognizable phenotype distinguishable from that of Bohring-Opitz syndrome.
evidence.explanation: The clinical delineation paper frames the causal alleles as loss of function.

hypotheses/0.description: Truncating ASXL3 alleles that trigger nonsense-mediated decay reduce ASXL3 message and protein, and the syndrome is described as caused by loss-of-function variants. This is the dosage model the pathophysiology chain is built on.

evidence.snippet: Statistical comparisons were made between individuals with variants leading to no protein product (nonsense-mediated messenger RNA decay [NMD], n = 87) and those with protein-truncating variants (no-NMD, n = 117).
evidence.explanation: Defines the two allele classes whose phenotypic divergence motivates this hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: Although autistic features were observed across all groups, the no-NMD and MCR2 cohorts had a higher proportion of individuals with formal autism diagnoses.
evidence.explanation: A phenotype difference tracking the NMD-escaping class, which argues the truncated protein is not silent.

evidence.snippet: Intellectual disability and global developmental delay were more severe in the NMD and MCR1 groups and were significant for the MCR1/MCR2 comparison
evidence.explanation: The same cohort's core severity measures run against this hypothesis. If a decay-escaping truncated protein were simply more toxic than a null, the decay-escaping class should carry the greater core burden; instead the decay-subject null class does. The difference could also track variant position or residual function rather than protein activity.

hypotheses/1.description: Truncating alleles that escape nonsense-mediated decay yield a stable C-terminally truncated ASXL3, and cohorts stratified by predicted decay differ in phenotype, which a pure dosage model does not predict. The original ASXL3 report already raised a dominant-negative reading of the truncated product. Whether the truncated protein is inert, dominant-negative, or gain of function has not been tested directly in patient material. The phenotype difference does not run uniformly in this hypothesis's favour: autistic features are enriched in the decay-escaping class, but the core severity measures are worse in the decay-subject null class, which is the opposite of what a straightforwardly more toxic truncated protein would predict. The mechanism is best read as a candidate modifier rather than as a symmetric competitor to the dosage model.

evidence.snippet: In this study, we utilize the frog, Xenopus laevis as a simpler and more accessible vertebrate neurodevelopmental model system to understand the embryological cause of Bainbridge-Ropers syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the model system whose translational validity to human heterozygous ASXL3 disease is the subject of this mismatch item.

open_questions/0.rationale: The strongest mechanistic link between the ASXL3 chromatin lesion and the neurodevelopmental phenotype comes from a morpholino knockdown in a frog embryo, which produces open neural plates and loss of hindbrain, primary neuron and neural crest markers - a far more dramatic patterning failure than anything seen in human patients, in whom GeneReviews notes that most individuals with seizures still have normal brain MRI. Two features of the model may explain the gap and limit translation: morpholino knockdown approaches a near-null state whereas human disease is heterozygous haploinsufficiency, and the human transcriptomic evidence comes from dermal fibroblasts rather than neural tissue. The translational validity of the cell-fate mechanism, not its existence in the model, is the open question.

evidence.snippet: the DNAm profiles of three individuals with ASXL3 variants were control-like
evidence.explanation: The sole empirical basis for the current belief that ASXL3 has no episignature - three individuals tested with a classifier built for a different gene - which is why this remains an open gap rather than a settled negative.

open_questions/1.rationale: The only relevant data come from applying an ASXL1/Bohring-Opitz classifier to three ASXL3 individuals, whose profiles were control-like. That is a negative result from a classifier built for a different gene on a very small sample, not evidence of absence. The question matters clinically because without an episignature there is no functional assay to reclassify ASXL3 variants of uncertain significance, which is precisely where the missense-variant question is unresolved.

evidence.snippet: substantial intrafamilial phenotypic variability, as well as the possibility of interfamilial phenotypic variability
evidence.explanation: Establishes variable expressivity across and within families carrying inherited ASXL3 variants.

evidence.snippet: The family reports emphasize the possibility of additional, yet currently unidentified, factors influencing phenotypic expression or, alternatively, may reflect uncertainty about the pathogenicity of inherited ASXL3 variants.
evidence.explanation: The authors explicitly refuse to separate reduced penetrance or modifier effects from pathogenicity uncertainty, which is why this is curated as an open gap rather than as a penetrance estimate.

evidence.snippet: Several gaps in our knowledge of this disorder were identified, namely, underlying pathophysiology and disease mechanism, disease contribution of missense variants, relevance of variant location, prevalence and penetrance data.
evidence.explanation: A systematic review names penetrance data as an explicit, unresolved knowledge gap.

open_questions/2.rationale: Almost the entire published cohort consists of de novo protein-truncating variants ascertained through severely affected probands, so penetrance has never been estimated against an unbiased denominator and a reader would reasonably but wrongly infer complete penetrance. The inherited-variant series reports substantial intrafamilial and possible interfamilial variability, with transmitting parents who are mildly affected or apparently unaffected. Critically, the authors decline to attribute this to reduced penetrance, offering instead the competing explanation that the inherited variants may not be pathogenic - an ambiguity that cannot be resolved without a functional assay, which is precisely what the absent episignature denies. Systematic review lists penetrance among the explicit unresolved gaps. This matters directly for counselling families in whom an ASXL3 variant is inherited rather than de novo.

evidence.snippet: Several gaps in our knowledge of this disorder were identified, namely, underlying pathophysiology and disease mechanism, disease contribution of missense variants, relevance of variant location, prevalence and penetrance data.
evidence.explanation: A systematic review names the disease contribution of missense variants as an explicit, unresolved knowledge gap.

open_questions/3.rationale: Every established BRPS variant is protein-truncating. Missense ASXL3 variants have been reported in autism cohorts without the severe syndromic features, and biallelic missense variants have been reported in a small number of individuals with congenital heart defects, but neither association is established. Systematic reviews list the disease contribution of missense variants as an explicit unresolved gap. Without an episignature or another functional assay there is currently no way to resolve individual missense variants of uncertain significance.

open_questions/4.rationale: Reduced ASXL3 expression is measured in patient cells and the syndrome is described as loss of function, but the largest cohort stratified by predicted nonsense-mediated decay finds phenotypic differences between decay-triggering and decay-escaping alleles, and the original report offered a dominant-negative reading of the truncated product. The cohort's core severity measures nonetheless run the other way, being worse in the decay-subject null class, and the one functional readout available in ASXL3 patient material shows increased H2AK119 ubiquitination, the loss-of-function direction and the opposite of the ASXL1 gain-of-function paradigm this hypothesis reasons from, though that measurement came from a decay-subject allele. No study has compared an NMD-escaping allele with a null in the same background, so the variant's functional_impact_category is recorded as UNKNOWN pending that comparison.

evidence.snippet: NKCC2 is responsible for carrying sodium from the tubular lumen into the cell coupled with potassium and chloride.
evidence.explanation: States the transport step NKCC2 occupies, which is the step lost in type I disease.

evidence.snippet: type I BS caused by mutations in NKCC2 (SLC12A1)
evidence.explanation: Assigns SLC12A1/NKCC2 loss of function to type I Bartter syndrome.

steps/6.description: SLC12A1 encodes NKCC2, the furosemide-sensitive apical cotransporter that carries Na+, K+ and Cl- together from the tubular lumen into the thick ascending limb cell. Biallelic loss of function removes the entry step of the transcellular NaCl pathway and defines type I Bartter syndrome.

evidence.snippet: K+ is recycled to the tubular lumen by the renal outer medullary K+ (ROMK) channel, also known as inwardly rectifying Kir1.1, encoded by KCNJ1 gene and which is located at the luminal surface of the epithelial cell.
evidence.explanation: States the recycling step ROMK occupies and its apical location in the thick ascending limb.

evidence.snippet: More than 40 KCNJ1 mutations, causing loss of function of ROMK channel, have been described
evidence.explanation: Establishes loss of ROMK function as the KCNJ1 disease mechanism.

steps/7.description: KCNJ1 encodes ROMK (Kir1.1), the apical channel that returns K+ to the tubular lumen. That recycling is what keeps luminal K+ available for NKCC2, so losing ROMK stalls the cotransporter indirectly rather than by disabling it. ROMK is also expressed in the cortical collecting duct, where it secretes K+ — which is why type II disease can show transient neonatal hyperkalaemia despite the salt-wasting phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Cl− can exit the cell via at least two specific basolateral chloride channels namely ClC-Ka and ClC-Kb (encoded by the CLCNKA and CLCNKB genes).
evidence.explanation: States the basolateral exit step that ClC-Kb occupies.

evidence.snippet: type III BS by mutations in CLC-Kb (CLCNKB)
evidence.explanation: Assigns CLCNKB loss of function to type III Bartter syndrome.

steps/8.description: CLCNKB encodes ClC-Kb, one of at least two basolateral chloride channels that let Cl- leave the thick ascending limb cell towards the interstitium. Biallelic loss of function blocks the exit step of the transcellular pathway and causes classic type III Bartter syndrome. ClC-Kb is expressed along the TAL, distal convoluted tubule and collecting-duct intercalated cells, which is consistent with the wide phenotypic range of this subtype.

evidence.snippet: MAGE-D2 encodes melanoma-associated antigen D2, which interacts with NKCC2 and increases their cell-surface expression and activity.
evidence.explanation: States the trafficking role that distinguishes this lesion from the transporter lesions of types I to IV.

evidence.snippet: This newly recognized form of BS is characterized in most cases by a very early onset of severe polyhydramnios and complete resolution of symptoms after birth.
evidence.explanation: Records the transient antenatal course that separates the MAGED2 form from the persistent subtypes.

steps/9.description: MAGED2 is not itself a transporter. It raises the cell-surface expression of NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb and of NCC in the distal convoluted tubule, so X-linked loss of function removes transporters from the membrane rather than disabling them in place. That is a distinct mechanism from the type I-IV channel and cotransporter lesions, and it matches the distinct clinical course: severe antenatal polyhydramnios followed by spontaneous resolution after birth.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in the BSND gene cause type IVa BS and result in impairment of barttin insertion in the plasma membrane of CLC-Kb and CLC-Ka channels in the Henle’s loop as well as in the inner ear, which interfere with epithelial salt transport.
evidence.explanation: Review links BSND-associated type 4A Bartter syndrome to defective ClC-K/barttin channel handling in both renal epithelia and inner ear.

evidence.snippet: type IVb is a digenic disorder with mutations in both CLCNKA and CLCNKB genes, which can lead to impairment in the functioning of two chloride channels and as a result, severe salt wasting and deafness.
evidence.explanation: Review supports the analogous type 4B mechanism in which dual ClC-K channel disruption produces both renal salt wasting and deafness.

steps/10.description: In type 4 Bartter syndrome, BSND loss-of-function or digenic CLCNKA/CLCNKB disruption impairs the ClC-K/barttin chloride-channel system shared by renal epithelia and the inner ear. This links the renal salt-wasting branch to the sensorineural-hearing branch without implying that all Bartter subtypes cause deafness.

evidence.snippet: The main ion channel at the luminal membrane is NKCC2 (furosemide-sensitive sodium–potassium–chloride cotransporter), which belongs to a family of sodium-coupled electrolyte transporters, encoded by the solute carrier family of SLC12A genes. NKCC2 is responsible for carrying sodium from the tubular lumen into the cell coupled with potassium and chloride.
evidence.explanation: Review describes the molecular physiology of NKCC2-mediated NaCl transport in the TAL that is disrupted in Bartter syndrome.

steps/11.description: The primary defect in Bartter syndrome is impaired sodium chloride reabsorption in the thick ascending limb (TAL) of the loop of Henle. NKCC2 (apical) mediates electroneutral entry of Na+, K+, and 2Cl-; ROMK recycles K+ back to the lumen to sustain NKCC2 activity; and ClC-Kb (with barttin) provides basolateral Cl- exit. Loss of any component disrupts the entire transcellular NaCl transport pathway.

evidence.snippet: patients with BS present hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism with normal/low blood pressure, reduced peripheral resistance, and hyporesponsiveness to antihypertensives.
evidence.explanation: Review describes the hyperaldosteronism with paradoxically normal/low blood pressure due to the tubular defect.

steps/12.description: Reduced NaCl reabsorption in the TAL increases sodium delivery to the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. Enhanced sodium reabsorption through ENaC in principal cells, driven by secondary hyperaldosteronism, creates a lumen-negative potential that drives potassium and hydrogen ion secretion, producing hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis.

evidence.snippet: In patients with BS, reduced reabsorption of chloride occurs due to the genetic defects, and an increase in chloride delivery to the macula densa with an abnormal volume sensing ensues. Therefore, the control of filtration becomes uncoupled from volume status.
evidence.explanation: Review explains the macula densa-mediated RAAS activation mechanism in Bartter syndrome.

steps/13.description: Chronic volume depletion from renal salt wasting stimulates the juxtaglomerular apparatus to increase renin secretion, resulting in hyperreninemia and secondary hyperaldosteronism. Despite elevated aldosterone, blood pressure remains normal or low because the primary renal tubular defect prevents effective sodium retention.

evidence.snippet: Henle’s loop has another important role in the reabsorption of divalent cations such as calcium (Ca2+) and magnesium (Mg2+), which are reabsorbed by a passive paracellular mechanism secondary to the driving force produced by active salt reabsorption.
evidence.explanation: Review explains the paracellular divalent cation reabsorption mechanism that is disrupted when TAL NaCl transport fails.

steps/14.description: NKCC2-mediated K+ recycling through ROMK generates a lumen-positive transepithelial voltage in the TAL that drives paracellular reabsorption of Ca2+ and Mg2+. Loss of this voltage in Types 1 and 2 causes hypercalciuria (leading to nephrocalcinosis) and hypomagnesemia.

evidence.snippet: Transepithelial salt movement into the medullary inter-stitium, together with the low permeability of the luminal membrane of the TAL to water, is important to allow the kidneys to develop interstitial hypertonicity and support the urinary concentrating ability.
evidence.explanation: Review explains the role of TAL NaCl reabsorption in maintaining the medullary osmotic gradient required for urinary concentration.

steps/15.description: NaCl reabsorption in the TAL is essential for generating the corticomedullary osmotic gradient required for urinary concentration. Impaired TAL transport reduces medullary tonicity, causing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus-like polyuria, polydipsia, and isosthenuria.

evidence.snippet: This impaired entry of sodium and chloride into the macula densa increases the expression of cyclooxygenase-2 (COX2) stimulating the renal production of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), also resulting in afferent arteriolar dilatation and activation of renin release by JGA.
evidence.explanation: Review describes the COX2/PGE2 pathway activation in Bartter syndrome and its role in amplifying RAAS activation.

steps/16.description: Hypokalemia and volume depletion stimulate renal prostaglandin E2 synthesis, which further inhibits NaCl reabsorption in the TAL and stimulates renin release, creating a positive feedback loop that amplifies salt wasting and electrolyte disturbances.

evidence.snippet: Nephrocalcinosis was constant in KCNJ1 and SLC12A1 but not in BSND and CLCNKB patients.
evidence.explanation: Cohort study confirms nephrocalcinosis is universal in Types 1 and 2 but absent in Types 3 and 4.

steps/17.description: Hypercalciuria from impaired paracellular calcium reabsorption in the TAL leads to medullary calcium deposition. Nephrocalcinosis is most prominent in Types 1 and 2 and is less common in Type 3.

evidence.snippet: In type IVa, barttin mutations impair potassium secretion in the stria vascularis and the vestibular labyrinth, whereas in type IVb mutations they occur in both chloride channels impairing their normal function in the inner ear.
evidence.explanation: Review describes the inner ear pathophysiology in both Type 4A and 4B Bartter syndrome.

steps/18.description: Barttin is co-expressed with ClC-Ka and ClC-Kb in the stria vascularis of the inner ear, where chloride channels are essential for endolymph potassium secretion. Loss of barttin (Type 4A) or both ClC-K channels (Type 4B) disrupts the endocochlear potential, causing sensorineural hearing loss.

evidence.snippet: Bartter syndrome (BS) is currently recognized as a rare inherited renal tubular disorder that affects around 1 in 1,000,000 of the population, caused by a defective salt reabsorption in the thick ascending limb (TAL) of loop of Henle, resulting in salt wasting, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis with relatively low levels of serum chloride.
evidence.explanation: Review defines the hallmark biochemical triad of Bartter syndrome.

steps/19.description: The biochemical hallmark of Bartter syndrome: persistent hypokalemia with hypochloremia and metabolic alkalosis resulting from renal potassium and chloride wasting.

evidence.snippet: BS is characterized by polyuria, failure to thrive, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperreninemia, and hyperaldosteronism.
evidence.explanation: Korean multicenter study listing hypokalemia as a cardinal feature.

steps/20.description: Renal potassium wasting due to enhanced distal K+ secretion driven by increased sodium delivery and hyperaldosteronism.

evidence.snippet: patients with BS present hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism with normal/low blood pressure
evidence.explanation: Review confirms hyperreninemia as a defining feature of Bartter syndrome.

steps/21.description: Elevated plasma renin activity due to chronic volume contraction and macula densa sensing of reduced luminal chloride.

evidence.snippet: BS is characterized by polyuria, failure to thrive, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperreninemia, and hyperaldosteronism.
evidence.explanation: Korean multicenter study confirms hyperaldosteronism as cardinal feature.

steps/22.description: Elevated aldosterone levels driven by hyperreninemia, contributing to potassium wasting and metabolic alkalosis.

evidence.snippet: all the ten hypercalciuric patients with aBS had nephrocalcinosis at the time of diagnosis and the last visit
evidence.explanation: Turkish cohort shows hypercalciuria in antenatal Bartter is consistently associated with nephrocalcinosis.

steps/23.description: Increased urinary calcium excretion due to loss of the lumen-positive potential driving paracellular calcium reabsorption in the TAL. Prominent in Types 1 and 2.

evidence.snippet: Henle’s loop has another important role in the reabsorption of divalent cations such as calcium (Ca2+) and magnesium (Mg2+), which are reabsorbed by a passive paracellular mechanism secondary to the driving force produced by active salt reabsorption.
evidence.explanation: Review evidence supports impaired paracellular magnesium reabsorption in Bartter syndrome as the mechanism for hypomagnesemia.

steps/24.description: Renal magnesium wasting from impaired paracellular magnesium reabsorption in the TAL.

evidence.snippet: severe salt wasting, hyposthenuria, increased production of PGE2, and failure to thrive
evidence.explanation: Review confirms increased PGE2 production as a feature of antenatal Bartter syndrome.

steps/25.description: Elevated urinary prostaglandin E2 excretion, particularly in antenatal forms. Contributes to fever, diarrhea, and vascular symptoms.

evidence.snippet: The onset of polyhydramnios, birth term, height and weight were similar for all groups
evidence.explanation: French cohort confirms polyhydramnios is consistent across all antenatal Bartter genotypes.

steps/26.description: Fetal polyuria from salt wasting causes polyhydramnios, typically presenting in the second or third trimester. Characteristic of antenatal forms (Types 1, 2, 4, 5).

evidence.snippet: Antenatal Bartter syndrome is characterized by severe polyhydramnios in mother leading to premature delivery.
evidence.explanation: Case report confirms premature delivery as a hallmark of antenatal Bartter syndrome.

steps/27.description: Polyhydramnios leads to premature labor and delivery, a major source of morbidity in antenatal Bartter syndrome.

evidence.snippet: This syndrome is associated with an increased antenatal and neonatal mortality because many patients fail to thrive.
evidence.explanation: Review confirms failure to thrive as a major feature of Bartter syndrome.

steps/28.description: Poor weight gain and growth failure from chronic electrolyte depletion and volume contraction.

evidence.snippet: At the last follow-up of 8 years after the initial diagnosis, 41% had short stature (height less than 3rd percentile)
evidence.explanation: Korean multicenter study quantifies frequency of short stature in Bartter syndrome patients.

steps/29.description: Growth retardation is common, particularly when diagnosis and treatment are delayed. In a Korean multicenter study, 41% had short stature at last follow-up.

evidence.snippet: BS is characterized by polyuria, failure to thrive, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperreninemia, and hyperaldosteronism.
evidence.explanation: Korean multicenter study lists polyuria as cardinal feature.

steps/30.description: Impaired urinary concentration due to loss of the medullary osmotic gradient. Can be severe and lead to dehydration.

evidence.snippet: Transepithelial salt movement into the medullary inter-stitium, together with the low permeability of the luminal membrane of the TAL to water, is important to allow the kidneys to develop interstitial hypertonicity and support the urinary concentrating ability.
evidence.explanation: Review evidence supports the TAL concentrating-gradient defect that produces polyuria and compensatory polydipsia in Bartter syndrome.

steps/31.description: Compensatory increased fluid intake in response to polyuria and volume depletion.

evidence.snippet: Postnatally newborns suffer from recurrent episodes of severe dehydration and electrolyte imbalance which can lead to fatal outcome.
evidence.explanation: Case report describes the severity of recurrent dehydration episodes in antenatal Bartter syndrome.

steps/32.description: Recurrent episodes of dehydration from salt and water wasting, especially in infancy.

evidence.snippet: Deafness at diagnosis was constant in patients with BSND mutations
evidence.explanation: French cohort confirms universal sensorineural deafness in Type 4A Bartter syndrome.

evidence.snippet: type IVb is a digenic disorder with mutations in both CLCNKA and CLCNKB genes, which can lead to impairment in the functioning of two chloride channels and as a result, severe salt wasting and deafness.
evidence.explanation: Review confirms deafness also occurs in Type 4B (digenic).

steps/33.description: Bilateral sensorineural deafness resulting from impaired chloride transport in the stria vascularis of the inner ear. Specific to Type 4 (barttin or digenic ClC-Ka/ClC-Kb mutations).

evidence.snippet: Despite management, a significant portion of this population exhibited growth impairment, while 11% developed CKD G3-G5.
evidence.explanation: Korean multicenter study documents CKD progression in 11% of 54 Bartter patients over median 8-year follow-up.

evidence.snippet: Three patients developed chronic renal failure: one with KCNJ1 mutations during the second decade of age and two with CLCNKB and BSND mutations and without nephrocalcinosis during the first year of life.
evidence.explanation: French cohort identifies CKD across genotypes, not always linked to nephrocalcinosis.

steps/34.description: A subset of Bartter syndrome patients develop chronic kidney disease over time, likely due to nephrocalcinosis, chronic hypokalemia, recurrent dehydration episodes, and long-term NSAID use. In a Korean multicenter study, 11% developed CKD G3-G5.

evidence.snippet: a 26-year-old man who presented with generalized body weakness and hypokalemia and was ultimately diagnosed with Bartter syndrome type II
evidence.explanation: Case report of late-onset Type 2 Bartter presenting with generalized weakness from hypokalemia.

steps/35.description: Hypokalemia-related skeletal muscle weakness, which can range from mild fatigue to severe episodic paralysis.

evidence.snippet: Although considered benign entities, major adverse cardiovascular events may complicate both syndromes, in form of ventricular arrhythmias leading to palpitations, syncope or sudden cardiac death, microvascular cardiac dysfunction and exercise-induced myocardial contractile deficit.
evidence.explanation: Narrative review highlights arrhythmic and cardiovascular complications of Bartter and Gitelman syndromes despite their usual normotensive phenotype.

steps/36.description: Chronic hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and neurohormonal abnormalities can produce clinically important cardiac arrhythmias in Bartter syndrome despite the usual absence of hypertension. Severe events may include syncope or sudden cardiac death.

evidence.snippet: Mutations of several genes encoding the transporters involved in salt reabsorption in the TAL cause different types of BS
evidence.explanation: Places the transporter lesions, NKCC2 among them, upstream of impaired TAL salt reabsorption.

edges/7.description: Losing the apical entry step abolishes electroneutral NaCl uptake and so the whole transcellular reabsorptive pathway of the thick ascending limb.

evidence.snippet: Mutations of several genes encoding the transporters involved in salt reabsorption in the TAL cause different types of BS
evidence.explanation: Places the ROMK lesion among the transporter defects that impair TAL salt reabsorption.

edges/8.description: Without luminal K+ recycling the NKCC2 cotransporter cannot sustain electroneutral NaCl entry, so type II disease reaches the same reabsorptive failure by a different step.

evidence.snippet: Mutations of several genes encoding the transporters involved in salt reabsorption in the TAL cause different types of BS
evidence.explanation: Places the ClC-Kb lesion among the transporter defects that impair TAL salt reabsorption.

edges/9.description: Chloride that cannot leave the cell basolaterally accumulates and the transcellular NaCl flux stops, producing the same reabsorptive failure from the opposite end of the cell to the type I lesion.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in MAGE-D2 reduce this expression of NKCC2 in the TAL and in the NCCT (thiazide-sensitive sodium chloride cotransporter), which is expressed in the DCT.
evidence.explanation: States the consequence of MAGED2 loss on NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb.

edges/10.description: Reduced NKCC2 at the apical membrane lowers the capacity of the same entry step that type I disease abolishes outright, which is why the phenotype is a transient rather than a permanent salt-wasting state.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in the BSND gene cause type IVa BS and result in impairment of barttin insertion in the plasma membrane of CLC-Kb and CLC-Ka channels in the Henle’s loop as well as in the inner ear, which interfere with epithelial salt transport.
evidence.explanation: The review explicitly places the ClC-K/barttin defect in Henle-loop epithelial salt transport, supporting the renal downstream edge.

edges/11.description: Defective ClC-K/barttin channel function in Henle-loop epithelia impairs epithelial salt transport, feeding into the renal NaCl reabsorption defect.

evidence.snippet: The sensory function of the inner ear becomes impaired in type IVa and IVb BS. In type IVa, barttin mutations impair potassium secretion in the stria vascularis and the vestibular labyrinth, whereas in type IVb mutations they occur in both chloride channels impairing their normal function in the inner ear.
evidence.explanation: The review directly links type 4A and 4B chloride-channel defects to impaired inner-ear sensory function.

edges/12.description: The same type 4 ClC-K/barttin channel system is required in the inner ear; barttin mutations impair potassium secretion in the stria vascularis and vestibular labyrinth, while dual ClC-K channel mutations impair inner-ear channel function.

evidence.snippet: This gene encodes the α1 subunit of the P/Q-type calcium channel Cav2.1, which is globally expressed in the brain and crucial for fast synaptic neurotransmission.

evidence.explanation: Confirms that CACNA1A variants cause cerebellar dysfunction through calcium channel disruption.

steps/1.description: CACNA1A encodes the pore-forming alpha-1A subunit of P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (Cav2.1). These channels are critical for calcium influx at presynaptic nerve terminals, particularly at cerebellar Purkinje cells and granule cell synapses. Pathogenic variants alter channel gating, trafficking, or expression, leading to disrupted neurotransmitter release and cerebellar dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: The spectrum of paroxysmal manifestations encompasses migraine with hemiplegic aura, episodic ataxia, epilepsy and paroxysmal non-epileptic movement disorders.
evidence.explanation: FHM1 with hemiplegic aura is a hallmark paroxysmal feature driven by gain-of-function CACNA1A variants and cortical spreading depression.

steps/2.description: Gain-of-function CACNA1A variants in FHM1 increase P/Q-type channel activity, leading to enhanced glutamate release from cortical pyramidal neurons. This creates a susceptibility to cortical spreading depression, the electrophysiological substrate of migraine aura, and may trigger episodes of hemiplegia through prolonged cortical inhibition.

evidence.snippet: SCA6 is underlined by an expanded polyglutamine tract in the C-terminal of the gene, a modification which does not primarily affect calcium currents
evidence.explanation: This distinguishes the SCA6 polyglutamine mechanism from primary P/Q-channel current dysfunction.

steps/3.description: SCA6 is caused by expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat in CACNA1A exon 47, encoding a polyglutamine tract in the cytoplasmic C-terminal domain of Cav2.1. Unlike other polyglutamine diseases, SCA6 expansions are relatively small (20-33 repeats). The cited evidence indicates that the expansion does not primarily alter P/Q-type calcium currents; this entry does not assert an aggregation or cell-death mechanism without direct supporting evidence.

evidence.snippet: We explored mitochondrial function and structure and observed that changes in mitochondrial structure preceded changes in function, and that mitochondrial function was not significantly altered at disease onset but was impaired later during disease progression.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that mitochondrial structural changes precede functional decline in SCA6 mouse model.

evidence.snippet: In addition, we observed impairment in mitophagy that exacerbates mitochondrial dysfunction at late disease stages.
evidence.explanation: Confirms impaired mitophagy as a contributor to disease progression in SCA6.

evidence.snippet: In post-mortem SCA6 patient cerebellar tissue, we observed metabolic changes that are consistent with mitochondrial impairments, supporting our results from animal models being translatable to human disease.
evidence.explanation: Post-mortem human data supports that mitochondrial dysfunction translates from the animal model to human SCA6.

steps/4.description: In SCA6, transcriptomic analysis reveals early downregulation of mitochondrial gene expression that precedes functional decline. As disease progresses, mitochondrial membrane potential declines, oxidative stress increases, and mitophagy becomes impaired, creating a feed-forward loop of organellar stress that contributes to Purkinje cell degeneration.

evidence.snippet: The spectrum of CACNA1A-related seizures is broad across both loss-of-function and gain-of-function variants and includes absence seizures, focal seizures with altered consciousness, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, tonic seizures, status epilepticus, and infantile spasms.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the broad seizure spectrum across both LOF and GOF variants.

evidence.snippet: About 49 (42.20%) patients had controlled seizures while 67 (57.80%) individuals remained with refractory seizures.

steps/5.description: In CACNA1A-related epilepsy and DEE, both gain-of-function and loss-of-function variants disrupt Cav2.1-dependent fast synaptic transmission. steps/1.description: Reduced FGFR3 receptor signaling is inferred from the kinase-domain substitutions, structural modeling, segregation and the overlap with null-animal phenotypes. The direction of effect is supported by model systems and expert curation, while allele-specific biochemical mechanisms remain unresolved.

evidence.explanation: Distinguishes the two pillar-cell developmental abnormalities in null mice.

steps/9.description: Fgfr3-null mice fail to develop inner pillar cells, while outer pillar-cell differentiation stalls and the tunnel of Corti fails to form. This provides a model-based explanation for human sensorineural hearing loss, but normal clinical CT/MRI does not demonstrate a pillar-cell defect in patients. Human hearing severity ranges from mild to severe and is not invariably profound.

evidence.snippet: growth plates in mutants were expanded and the columnar morphology of chondrocytes was lost
evidence.explanation: Direct histology of disordered mouse growth plates.

evidence.snippet: the collagen fibers lost its symmetry with disrupted organization in fgfr3 mutant chondrocytes
evidence.explanation: Cartilage-matrix organization in fish.

steps/10.description: Conditional Fgfr3 loss disrupts columnar organization and chondrocyte polarity, including primary-cilium orientation, in mouse growth plates. Mutant fish also show disordered chondrocyte arrangement and cartilage collagen organization. These structural abnormalities can contribute to cartilage dysplasia and chondroma-like lesions.

evidence.snippet: We have identified a role for fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR-3) in this process by disrupting the murine Fgfr-3 gene to produce severe and progressive bone dysplasia with enhanced and prolonged endochondral bone growth.
evidence.explanation: Establishes enhanced and prolonged endochondral growth as the tissue-level result of losing the receptor.

evidence.snippet: Radiographic findings included tall vertebral bodies with irregular borders and broad femoral metaphyses with long tubular shafts
evidence.explanation: The human radiographic counterpart of the mouse overgrowth phenotype.

evidence.snippet: These findings indicate that abnormal FGFR3 signaling can cause human anomalies by promoting as well as inhibiting endochondral bone growth.
evidence.explanation: States the bidirectional axis that makes this entry the counterpart of the achondroplasia group.

steps/11.description: Increased growth-plate output lengthens long bones and vertebral bodies. Human radiographs show tall vertebrae and broad femoral metaphyses with long shafts. Altered vertebral growth may contribute to spinal deformity, but the mechanical sequence has not been established in patients. The disease is not restricted categorically to endochondral bones: cranial findings and fish intramembranous-ossification defects require separate consideration.

evidence.snippet: Both the frontal suture and coronal suture were not closed even at adult stage in fgfr3 mutants.
evidence.explanation: Delayed suture closure in fish.

evidence.snippet: the delayed intramembranous ossification of opercle and branchiostegal rays was not significantly changed in XAV939-treated mutants
evidence.explanation: Negative treatment readout distinct from improved cartilage architecture.

steps/12.description: Fgfr3-mutant zebrafish show delayed cranial mineralization, persistent sutures and separate small bone islands. These findings offer a model for sutural abnormalities such as human Wormian bones; they do not establish a cause of intellectual disability or all human microcephaly. Wnt inhibition did not significantly restore intramembranous ossification.

evidence.snippet: we found that postnatal chondrocyte-specific Fgfr3 deletion induced multiple chondroma-like lesions, including enchondromas and osteochondromas, adjacent to disordered growth plates.
evidence.explanation: The model-system observation of cartilage lesions arising from Fgfr3 loss.

evidence.snippet: Several affected individuals had a single osteochondroma of the femur, the tibia, or a phalanx
evidence.explanation: The human counterpart. Graded INDIRECT because the report records the lesions without linking them to FGFR3 signaling in those individuals.

steps/13.description: Disordered growth plates lacking FGFR3 generate enchondroma- and osteochondroma-like cartilage lesions in mice. Several members of the Utah pedigree had a solitary osteochondroma of the femur, tibia or a phalanx, which is the human observation this node is anchored to. The link between the two is not established: the human lesions are solitary and were not examined for hedgehog activity, while the mouse lesions are multiple and mechanistically dissected, so the node records a plausible correspondence rather than a demonstrated one.

evidence.snippet: we found an extra row of outer hair cells, and accompanying Deiters' cells, in the apical two thirds of the organ of Corti in the Fgfr3 mutant.
evidence.explanation: Direct mouse cochlear patterning result.

steps/14.description: Fgfr3-null mice develop an additional row of outer hair cells and accompanying Deiters cells in the apical two thirds of the organ of Corti. FGFR3 therefore regulates sensory/supporting-cell patterning as well as pillar-cell differentiation. The relative contribution of each lesion to hearing loss has not been separated in human CATSHL.

evidence.snippet: Adult height in males was >97th percentile in 5 of 5 men, with a mean height of 77 inches, and adult height in females was >75th percentile in 9 of 9 and >97th percentile in 8 of 9 women, with a mean height of 70 inches.
evidence.explanation: Gives per-sex counts above the 97th and 75th centiles, supporting a VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/15.description: Marked postnatal overgrowth is characteristic but variable. In the Utah adult subset, 13/14 measured adults exceeded the 97th centile; one woman was between the 75th and 97th centiles. The Italian proband had normal birth length with growth above the 97th centile from infancy. Average stature was reported in an additional candidate spectrum case with homozygous Asn540Asp.

evidence.snippet: On audiological exam, each tested individual had bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and absent otoacoustic emissions
evidence.explanation: Establishes the sensorineural character and the absent otoacoustic emissions.

evidence.snippet: By report, the hearing loss was congenital or developed in early infancy, progressed variably in early childhood, and ranged from mild to severe.
evidence.explanation: Infantile onset and variable early progression in the founding pedigree; later families expand onset into childhood.

evidence.snippet: We report the case of a 12-year-old girl and her father who both had marked postnatal tall stature, camptodactyly and clinodactyly, scoliosis and juvenile-onset hearing loss.
evidence.explanation: Childhood-onset hearing loss in the Arg621Cys family broadens onset beyond infancy.

steps/16.description: All formally tested affected members of the Utah pedigree had bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with absent otoacoustic emissions. Fourteen of 20 had documented hearing loss and three additional relatives reported hearing loss without formal testing; 17/20 therefore describes any reported/documented loss, not 17 proven bilateral sensorineural cases. Onset ranged from congenital/early infancy in that family to childhood in later reports; progression was variable, and severity ranged from mild to severe.

evidence.snippet: pectus abnormalities; and/or severe thoracolumbar kyphoscoliosis
evidence.explanation: Records the severe end of the spinal phenotype.

steps/17.description: Spinal curvature can progress to severe thoracolumbar kyphoscoliosis. The Utah series included an approximately 80-degree lumbar curvature; the Arg621Cys father underwent spinal surgery at 23 years. Altered skeletal growth may contribute, but the precise biomechanical sequence is not established.

evidence.snippet: microcephaly, wormian skull bones, a high palate
evidence.explanation: Same feature list. Graded HUMAN_CLINICAL for the same reason; no denominator, so no frequency band.

steps/18.description: Supernumerary sutural skull bones have been reported, including in the homozygous Thr546Lys family. Irregular cranial bone islands in mutant fish offer a partial anatomical analogue.

evidence.snippet: Several affected individuals had a single osteochondroma of the femur, the tibia, or a phalanx
evidence.explanation: Records the lesion and its sites; no denominator is given, so no frequency band.

evidence.snippet: Radiographic findings included tall vertebral bodies with irregular borders

steps/20.description: Increased vertebral body height with irregular borders on radiographs - the axial-skeleton counterpart of the long-bone overgrowth.

evidence.snippet: broad femoral metaphyses with long tubular shafts
evidence.explanation: Direct radiographic description of the metaphyseal phenotype.

steps/21.description: Broad femoral metaphyses with long tubular shafts.

evidence.snippet: The clinical picture is characterized by tall stature and severe skeletal abnormalities leading to inability to walk, with camptodactyly, arachnodactyly, and scoliosis.
evidence.explanation: Reports arachnodactyly in the biallelic family.

steps/22.description: Long slender digits, reported in the two brothers homozygous for p.Thr546Lys.

evidence.snippet: We mapped the locus causing a novel disorder characterized by camptodactyly, tall stature, scoliosis, and hearing loss (CATSHL syndrome) to chromosome 4p.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the 4p locus that contains FGFR3 and led to the gene assignment.

genes/0.notes: ClinGen classifies the semidominant FGFR3-CATSHL relationship as Moderate (reevaluation 24 August 2026). Classic pedigrees involve Arg621His, Arg621Cys and homozygous Thr546Lys. Additional missense observations from tall-stature and hearing-loss cohorts broaden the candidate spectrum but do not establish equal clinical or mechanistic certainty for every allele. The evidence supports a reported relationship whose definitive validity has not yet been established.

evidence.snippet: Early recognition and treatment of hearing impairment may improve outcomes, including speech and language development
evidence.explanation: NHGRI clinical-care summary for the FGFR3 group including CATSHL; management rationale, not a CATSHL treatment trial.

evidence.snippet: Other treatment interventions may include antiseizure medications, hearing aids, and individualized developmental support.
evidence.explanation: General FGFR3 skeletal-dysplasia supportive care; only hearing aids are used to support this intervention.

treatments/0.description: Audiological evaluation and hearing amplification are supportive management options for sensorineural loss. FGFR3 clinical-care resources recommend early recognition and treatment of hearing impairment, but the cited sources do not provide CATSHL-specific hearing-aid outcome estimates.

evidence.snippet: He had thoracic scoliosis that required spinal surgery at the age of 23.
evidence.explanation: Cannova et al. document surgery in the affected father.

treatments/1.description: Spinal surgery was performed at age 23 for scoliosis in the Italian Arg621Cys father. The case establishes use, not comparative effectiveness or a standardized CATSHL surgical protocol.

evidence.snippet: Mother and father are mildly affected with slight tall stature, relative microcephaly, and long lower limbs.
evidence.explanation: ClinGen family abstraction supports counseling that heterozygous phenotype need not be completely absent. The Mendelian genotype probabilities are conditional inferences.

treatments/2.description: Counseling depends on the allele, parental genotype and uncertain penetrance. A heterozygous dominant-associated allele has a 50% transmission probability per pregnancy; if both parents carry the same recessive-associated allele, each pregnancy has a 25% probability of homozygosity. These are conditional genotype probabilities, not guarantees of phenotype or severity. Subtle heterozygous manifestations and the Moderate gene-disease validity assessment should inform interpretation.

evidence.snippet: Other treatment interventions may include antiseizure medications, hearing aids, and individualized developmental support.
evidence.explanation: General FGFR3-disorder review supports individualized developmental care, not a disease-specific effect estimate.

treatments/3.description: Individualized developmental support is a general supportive-care option when delay or learning difficulties are present; no CATSHL-specific efficacy study is reported in the cited review.

evidence.snippet: there were no chondroma-like lesions in the mutants after 4 weeks of SMOi treatment
evidence.explanation: Mouse lesion prevention with GDC-0449/vismodegib.

evidence.snippet: adverse secondary effects were induced, including premature growth plate fusion leading to a shorter long bone
evidence.explanation: Developmental toxicity limits therapeutic interpretation.

treatments/4.description: Vismodegib prevented chondroma-like lesions in conditional Fgfr3-deficient mice during a four-week treatment window. The same intervention induced premature growth-plate fusion and reduced long-bone length in controls and mutants. This is a preclinical pathway experiment with important developmental toxicity, not demonstrated CATSHL treatment.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Smoothened inhibition reduces Hedgehog signaling in the mouse experiment.

evidence.snippet: The abnormal arrangement and hypertrophy of chondrocytes in ceratohyal cartilage were both alleviated in XAV939-treated mutants.
evidence.explanation: Partial cartilage rescue.

evidence.snippet: the delayed intramembranous ossification of opercle and branchiostegal rays was not significantly changed in XAV939-treated mutants
evidence.explanation: No significant rescue of the distinct intramembranous-ossification readout.

treatments/5.description: XAV939 exposure at 2.5 micromolar from 10–20 days post fertilization partly improved cranial/cartilage abnormalities in fgfr3-mutant zebrafish. Delayed intramembranous ossification was not significantly corrected. This is a preclinical partial rescue and does not establish human efficacy or safety.

treatments/5/targets/0.description: XAV939 promotes beta-catenin degradation through axin stabilization in the fish experiment.

evidence.snippet: The reason for the discrepant in the craniofacial phenotypes between mouse model and patients remains to be studied.
evidence.explanation: The authors state the mismatch explicitly and record it as unresolved. Quoted as written, including the grammatical slip in the original.

evidence.snippet: craniofacial bone malformation with microcephaly and delayed closure of cranial sutures
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the zebrafish, unlike the mouse, does show the craniofacial phenotype.

open_questions/0.rationale: The 2020 study reports that the then-characterized Fgfr3-deficient mouse models lacked an apparent craniofacial skeletal phenotype, while its zebrafish model had cranial malformation and delayed sutural closure. Fish cartilage and osteoblast readouts support distinct developmental contributions, and Wnt inhibition partly improved cartilage but not intramembranous ossification. These findings do not establish the basis of human intellectual disability or prove that every mouse model lacks every cranial abnormality. Relative microcephaly in a very tall individual must also be distinguished from absolute microcephaly.

evidence.snippet: For several reasons, it is unlikely that the loss of function caused by p.R621H results from haploinsufficiency.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own framing of the mechanism as an inference from exclusion rather than a demonstration.

open_questions/1.rationale: The original Arg621His report inferred a dominant-negative mechanism from structural modeling, expression/localization observations and comparisons with null genotypes. It did not demonstrate mutant/wild-type heterodimer inhibition. ClinGen retains this as a proposed mechanism. Direct measurements of variant-specific kinase activity and signaling in relevant tissues are needed to distinguish hypomorphic, dominant-negative and context-dependent effects, including for the later candidate alleles.

evidence.snippet: The inner ear defect is mainly associated with an increased number of pillar cells or modified supporting cells in the organ of Corti.
evidence.explanation: Shows the gain-of-function receptor producing the opposite cellular change in the same structure, which is what makes the bidirectional failure a real question rather than a rhetorical one.

evidence.snippet: The mutant Fgfr3(Y367C/+) mice exhibit fully penetrant deafness with a significantly elevated auditory brainstem response threshold for all frequencies tested.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the activating allele also causes deafness, not merely a cellular change.

open_questions/2.rationale: Loss of Fgfr3 abolishes pillar cell differentiation; the activating Y367C allele produces fully penetrant deafness with an increased number of pillar or modified supporting cells. The organ of Corti therefore fails in both directions from an intermediate optimum, which is unusual and is not explained by a simple dose-response model of the receptor. Whether the two deafnesses share a final common lesion or are distinct failures of the same patterning step is unknown, and the answer would constrain how the human hearing loss is expected to progress.

evidence.snippet: A missense mutation in fibulin-5, encoding a widely expressed constituent of the extracellular matrix that has an essential role in elastic fibre assembly and has been shown to cause cutis laxa, was detected as the only novel non-synonymous sequence variant within the disease interval.
evidence.explanation: Sources both the fibulin-5 elastic-fibre role and its identification as the segregating variant in the CMT-linked interval.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, it adumbrates a new syndrome by linking concurrent pathologic alterations affecting peripheral nerves, eyes and skin to mutations in the fibulin-5 gene.
evidence.explanation: Supports the multi-tissue extracellular-matrix reading of the FBLN5 phenotype recorded in this node.

steps/5.description: FBLN5 encodes fibulin-5, a widely expressed extracellular matrix constituent with an essential role in elastic fibre assembly; loss-of-function alleles cause cutis laxa. Heterozygous missense variants segregate with demyelinating CMT, and the same variant class produces concurrent pathology in eye and skin, which is why FBLN5 families combine neuropathy with macular degeneration and hyperextensible skin. The step from an elastic-fibre defect to Schwann-cell demyelination is not established by the cited work, and is recorded here as an unexplained gap rather than asserted.

evidence.snippet: Altered Ca2+ -transients in p.Val615Met patient fibroblasts suggested that the variant has a dominant-negative effect on inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor type 3 function.
evidence.explanation: The functional measurement behind the calcium-release dysregulation asserted by this node.

evidence.snippet: Together with two previously identified variants, our report adds further evidence that ITPR3 is a disease-causing gene for CMT and indicates altered Ca2+ homeostasis in disease pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own statement that altered calcium homeostasis is the implicated pathogenic mechanism.

steps/6.description: ITPR3 encodes the type 3 inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor, an endoplasmic-reticulum calcium release channel. Fibroblasts from a patient carrying the dominant p.Val615Met variant show altered calcium transients, which the authors interpret as a dominant-negative effect on receptor function, implicating altered calcium homeostasis in the demyelinating neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: The most common genetic diagnosis was PMP22 duplication (CMT1A; 505/1165, 43.3%)
evidence.explanation: Establishes PMP22 duplication / CMT1A as the dominant genetic cause of demyelinating CMT.

steps/7.description: The most common cause of CMT (CMT1A) is a 1.4 Mb tandem duplication of chromosome 17p11.2 containing the peripheral myelin protein 22 (PMP22) gene. PMP22 overexpression destabilizes compact myelin and disrupts the structural organization of the myelin sheath, causing dysmyelination, demyelination, and characteristic onion-bulb formation from repeated Schwann-cell remyelination attempts. Slowed nerve conduction follows, and chronic secondary axonal loss eventually drives the clinical phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in the MPZ gene can lead to protein misfolding, unfolded protein response (UPR), endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, or protein mistrafficking.
evidence.explanation: Establishes UPR / ER stress as the canonical CMT1B disease mechanism.

steps/8.description: MPZ (myelin protein zero) mutations cause CMT1B. Many MPZ variants produce protein misfolding that triggers the unfolded protein response (UPR) and chronic endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress in Schwann cells, or cause mistrafficking of the mutant protein. The resulting myelin instability drives the demyelinating CMT1B phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Most GJB1 mutations cause disability through the loss of function of Cx32
evidence.explanation: Establishes loss of function of connexin-32 (Cx32) as the dominant CMTX1 disease mechanism.

steps/9.description: GJB1 mutations cause loss of function of connexin-32, which forms reflexive gap-junction channels across the non-compact myelin of the paranodes and Schmidt-Lanterman incisures, shortening the radial diffusion pathway between the Schwann-cell body and the adaxonal cytoplasm. Loss of these channels impairs Schwann-cell homeostasis and myelin maintenance, producing the X-linked demyelinating-spectrum neuropathy CMTX1.

evidence.snippet: Typically, the pathophysiology of CMTX1 includes features of both demyelination and axon loss
evidence.explanation: Supports the convergence of demyelinating CMT mechanisms on combined demyelination and secondary axonal loss.

steps/10.description: The shared terminal node of the demyelinating compartment. Primary Schwann-cell and myelin defects (PMP22 dosage, MPZ misfolding, connexin-32 gap-junction failure) converge on segmental demyelination and repeated remyelination (onion-bulb formation), which over time produces length-dependent secondary axonal degeneration. It is this secondary axonal loss, affecting the longest motor and sensory fibers first, that determines the progressive clinical deficit shared with the axonal compartment.

evidence.snippet: The predominant clinical signs were muscle weakness and wasting in the lower limbs.
evidence.explanation: 119-case CMT1A study identifies distal lower-limb muscle weakness as the predominant clinical sign.

evidence.snippet: None of the patients was normal on clinical examination and all presented at least pes cavus or ankle jerk areflexia.
evidence.explanation: In a 119-case CMT1A cohort, every patient had at least pes cavus or ankle areflexia on examination.

evidence.snippet: None of the patients was normal on clinical examination and all presented at least pes cavus or ankle jerk areflexia.
evidence.explanation: Ankle-jerk areflexia was a near-universal examination finding in this CMT1A cohort.

evidence.snippet: Sensory potentials were abnormal in all cases, even where there was no clinical sensory loss.
evidence.explanation: Sensory nerve potentials were abnormal in all CMT1A cases, evidencing the sensory component of the neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: Motor nerve conduction velocity (MNCV) was uniformly reduced in all nerves, and was < or = 33 m/s in the median nerve for all patients.
evidence.explanation: A 119-case CMT1A cohort directly reports uniformly reduced motor nerve conduction velocity.

steps/15.description: Uniformly slowed motor nerve conduction is the defining electrophysiologic feature of the demyelinating CMT1 compartment.

edges/5.description: PMP22-dosage-driven dysmyelination produces demyelination and, over time, length-dependent secondary axonal degeneration.

edges/6.description: Misfolded-MPZ-driven Schwann-cell ER stress destabilizes myelin, producing demyelination and secondary axonal degeneration.

edges/7.description: Connexin-32 gap-junction failure impairs Schwann-cell homeostasis, producing demyelination together with axon loss in CMTX1.

edges/8.description: FBLN5 variants segregate with demyelinating CMT, so the extracellular matrix defect is upstream of the shared demyelinating terminal node; the intervening Schwann-cell steps are not established in the cited work.

edges/9.description: Dysregulated inositol-trisphosphate-receptor calcium release precedes the demyelinating neuropathy with secondary axonal features seen in ITPR3 families; the intervening steps are not established in the cited work.

evidence.snippet: Motor nerve conduction velocity (MNCV) was uniformly reduced in all nerves, and was < or = 33 m/s in the median nerve for all patients.
evidence.explanation: The CMT1A cohort directly supports slowed motor nerve conduction as the electrophysiologic consequence of the demyelinating CMT1 lesion.

edges/10.description: Segmental demyelination slows saltatory conduction across peripheral nerves.

evidence.snippet: The predominant clinical signs were muscle weakness and wasting in the lower limbs.
evidence.explanation: The 119-case CMT1A cohort identifies distal lower-limb weakness and wasting as predominant clinical signs.

edges/11.description: Length-dependent secondary axonal loss in motor fibers produces distal lower-limb weakness and wasting.

evidence.snippet: None of the patients was normal on clinical examination and all presented at least pes cavus or ankle jerk areflexia.
evidence.explanation: The cohort supports pes cavus as a common examination finding in CMT1A.

edges/12.description: Chronic distal motor imbalance from hereditary peripheral neuropathy produces cavus foot deformity.

evidence.snippet: None of the patients was normal on clinical examination and all presented at least pes cavus or ankle jerk areflexia.
evidence.explanation: The cohort supports ankle-jerk areflexia as a CMT1A examination finding.

edges/13.description: Peripheral demyelinating neuropathy and secondary axonal dysfunction reduce ankle tendon reflexes.

evidence.snippet: Sensory potentials were abnormal in all cases, even where there was no clinical sensory loss.
evidence.explanation: Abnormal sensory potentials in all cases support sensory-fiber involvement in CMT1A.

edges/14.description: Sensory fiber involvement in the demyelinating neuropathy produces distal sensory impairment.

evidence.snippet: The most common genetic diagnosis was PMP22 duplication (CMT1A; 505/1165, 43.3%)
evidence.explanation: PMP22 duplication is the dominant genetic cause of demyelinating CMT.

genes/0.notes: A 1.4 Mb tandem duplication of 17p11.2 containing PMP22 causes CMT1A, the single most common CMT genotype. PMP22 point mutations cause rarer demyelinating forms; the reciprocal deletion causes HNPP (curated separately).

evidence.snippet: Mutations in the MPZ gene can lead to protein misfolding, unfolded protein response (UPR), endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, or protein mistrafficking.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the MPZ misfolding / ER-stress mechanism in CMT1B.

genes/1.notes: MPZ (myelin protein zero) is the most abundant peripheral myelin protein. Mutations cause CMT1B; many trigger protein misfolding, UPR, and chronic ER stress in Schwann cells.

evidence.explanation: GJB1 / CMTX1 is the second most common genetically resolved CMT subtype.

genes/2.notes: GJB1 encodes connexin-32, expressed in Schwann cells at the paranodal gap junctions and Schmidt-Lanterman incisures. X-linked (CMTX1), the second most common genetic cause of CMT.

evidence.snippet: Stable expression of Egr2 is specifically associated with the onset of myelination in the peripheral nervous system (PNS).
evidence.explanation: Establishes EGR2 (Krox20) as a Schwann-cell transcription factor controlling PNS myelination, the process disrupted in demyelinating CMT1D.

genes/3.notes: EGR2 (Krox20) is a transcription factor required for Schwann-cell myelination. Dominant mutations cause demyelinating CMT1D; recessive and other variants cause congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy and Dejerine-Sottas neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: This study identifies fibulin-5 as a gene involved in Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathies and reveals heterozygous fibulin-5 mutations in 2% of our patients with age-related macular degeneration.
evidence.explanation: Establishes FBLN5 as a CMT gene.

evidence.snippet: FBLN5 | HGNC:3602 | demyelinating hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy | MONDO:0018776 | AD | Moderate
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the FBLN5 demyelinating-neuropathy relationship as Moderate with autosomal dominant inheritance, the strength recorded in these notes.

genes/4.notes: Heterozygous FBLN5 missense variants cause demyelinating CMT (CMT1H). The relationship was established by mapping a dominant CMT1 family to chromosome 14q32 and resequencing the interval, then finding two further missense variants among 112 unclassified CMT probands. ClinGen's Charcot-Marie-Tooth Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel classifies FBLN5 as Moderate for demyelinating hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy, so this is a supported but not definitively established gene-disease relationship.

evidence.snippet: Exome sequencing identified a heterozygous ITPR3 p.Val615Met variant segregating with the disease.
evidence.explanation: The segregating variant in the dominant family behind this gene-disease relationship.

evidence.snippet: Trio exome sequencing identified a de novo ITPR3 variant p.Arg2524Cys.
evidence.explanation: The independent de novo variant that supports the relationship beyond the single family.

evidence.snippet: The individual who was the only affected in his family had disease onset at age 4 with demyelinating neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: Sources the much earlier onset of the de novo case recorded in this subtype's description.

genes/5.notes: Autosomal dominant ITPR3 variants cause CMT1J. The gene-disease relationship rests on a segregating p.Val615Met variant in a four-affected dominant family, a de novo p.Arg2524Cys variant in an isolated case, two previously identified variants, and a dominant-negative calcium-transient phenotype in patient fibroblasts. A search of the approved symbol ITPR3 in the ClinGen Gene-Disease Validity CSV (snapshot 2026-08-13) returns no row, so no expert panel has yet classified this relationship.

treatments/0.description: Mainstay of supportive care to maintain mobility and function.

treatments/1.description: Ankle-foot orthoses to compensate for foot drop and improve gait.

treatments/2.description: Counseling for affected individuals and families.

evidence.snippet: Compounds such as PXT3003, which are being clinically and preclinically investigated, and a broad array of therapeutic agents and their corresponding mechanisms are discussed.
evidence.explanation: Establishes PXT3003 as an active clinical/preclinical therapeutic candidate for CMT1A.

treatments/3.description: Oral fixed-dose combination of low-dose baclofen, naltrexone, and sorbitol designed to lower PMP22 expression and improve axonal function in CMT1A. Phase III trials (PLEO-CMT NCT02579759 completed, PREMIER NCT04762758).

treatments/3/targets/0.description: PXT3003 is designed to lower PMP22 expression, targeting the primary dysmyelinating lesion of CMT1A.

evidence.snippet: point mutations or small insertions and deletions (indels) usually cause CMT type 1E (CMT1E) or HNPP
evidence.explanation: Defines the CMT1E lesion class as point mutations and indels, separating it from the duplication that causes CMT1A.

steps/1.description: A heterozygous coding point mutation or small indel, usually in one of the conserved transmembrane domains, produces an abnormal PMP22 protein. This is the point of departure from CMT1A and HNPP, both of which alter the amount of a normal protein rather than its sequence.

evidence.snippet: disease-related missense mutations within transmembrane domains of PMP22 disturb intracellular protein trafficking leading to accumulation of the mutant protein in the endoplasmic reticulum/Golgi compartment
evidence.explanation: States the trafficking lesion and locates it to the transmembrane domains. This paper's own subject is the PMP22-integrin complex and the basal lamina; the quoted sentence is its framing of established PMP22 mutation biology, so it is graded BACKGROUND rather than PRIMARY_RESULT.

steps/2.description: The mutant protein does not traffic to the Schwann cell plasma membrane. It accumulates in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi compartment instead, and the trafficking defect is attributable specifically to mutations within the transmembrane domains.

evidence.snippet: heterologous PMP22 expression increases the amplitude of currents similar to those ascribed to store-operated calcium (SOC) channels, particularly those involving transient receptor canonical channel 1 (TrpC1).
evidence.explanation: The electrophysiological measurement. Graded INDIRECT because it establishes that PMP22 modulates these currents, not that a CMT1E allele's effect on them causes disease; the authors' own framing is that the role of PMP22 in Schwann cell physiology is not well understood.

steps/3.description:
A third consequence of the mutant protein, on a different axis from proteostasis and lipid trafficking. PMP22 modulates store-operated calcium channel activity: heterologous expression increases currents resembling those carried by store-operated channels, particularly TRPC1. A PMP22 whose amount or sequence is abnormal therefore changes Schwann-cell calcium handling as well as its own disposal and its lipid environment.
Marked PROVISIONAL and drawn as an INDIRECT edge. The measurement is in a heterologous expression system, and it is about PMP22 rather than about a CMT1E allele specifically, so its weight for this disease is inferential.

evidence.snippet: PMP22 has an extended half-life and forms aggresome-like structures that are surrounded by molecular chaperones and lysosomes
evidence.explanation: The observation in Trembler-J nerve that defines this node: not merely retained protein but an organized aggresome under chaperone and lysosomal surveillance.

steps/4.description: Retained PMP22 has an extended half-life and forms aggresome-like structures surrounded by molecular chaperones and lysosomes. Clearance depends on autophagy: it is enhanced when autophagy is activated and largely prevented when autophagy is inhibited. The Schwann cell is therefore holding the mutant protein under a disposal system that can be saturated.

evidence.snippet: In Schwann cells from homozygous Trembler J (TrJ) mice carrying a Leu16Pro mutation, cholesterol was retained with TrJ-PMP22 in the Golgi, alongside a corresponding reduction in its plasma membrane level.
evidence.explanation: The measured cholesterol mis-localization in a cell model of the human Leu16Pro allele, with the reciprocal fall at the plasma membrane.

evidence.snippet: PMP22 overexpression, which models CMT1A caused by gene duplication, triggered cholesterol sequestration to lysosomes, and reduced ATP-binding cassette transporter-dependent cholesterol efflux.
evidence.explanation: The CMT1A comparison from the same study. Quoted here because it is what makes the Golgi localization specific to the point-mutation disease rather than a generic PMP22 phenomenon.

steps/5.description:
Cholesterol is retained with the mutant protein in the Golgi, and plasma-membrane cholesterol falls correspondingly. Because cholesterol is a structural lipid of compact myelin, this diverts a myelin building block away from the membrane where it is needed.
Note the source paper contrasts this directly with the CMT1A mechanism in the same experiments: PMP22 overexpression sequesters cholesterol to lysosomes instead. The two PMP22 diseases therefore mis-route the same lipid to different compartments, which is a sharper statement of "different mechanism" than a severity comparison would be.

evidence.snippet: Administration of curcumin significantly decreases the percentage of apoptotic Schwann cells and results in increased number and size of myelinated axons
evidence.explanation: A rescue result cited as validation of the mechanism it targets, which is an inference step: reducing apoptosis improves myelination, so apoptosis is upstream of the myelination failure. Graded INDIRECT for that reason, and MODEL_ORGANISM because the quoted measurement is in the Trembler-J mouse.

steps/6.description: Proteostatic burden and diverted myelin lipid converge on the myelinating Schwann cell, which undergoes apoptosis and fails to make and maintain normal compact myelin. That apoptosis is the convergence point is supported by the curcumin result, where reducing ER-retention-associated apoptosis increased the number and size of myelinated axons.

evidence.snippet: In TrJ nerves, laminin is modestly increased while full-length forms of collagen IV and fibronectin are decreased.
evidence.explanation: The measured basement-membrane changes, which is what "remodelling" means here rather than a general inflammatory description.

evidence.snippet: macrophages are a significant source of both MMP-2 and MMP-9.
evidence.explanation: Attributes the enzymes to infiltrating macrophages, which is the basis for binding a macrophage cell type on this node rather than treating the remodelling as Schwann-cell-autonomous.

steps/7.description:
The inflammatory arm, and the only route in this entry to a cellular participant other than the Schwann cell. In Trembler-J nerve the basement membrane is remodelled - laminin modestly increased, full-length collagen IV and fibronectin decreased - with MMP-2 and MMP-9 detectable and gelatinolytic activity up. The paper attributes a significant share of both enzymes to infiltrating macrophages.
This matters because the rest of the pathograph is Schwann-cell-autonomous, so without this node the entry would imply that nothing else participates in the nerve pathology.
