evidence.explanation: Documents short middle phalanges in a molecularly confirmed patient.

steps/11.description: Shortened middle phalanges, reported in the same molecularly confirmed patient as the skin syndactyly.

evidence.snippet: Short stature and dislocation/subluxation of hip joint are consistently observed.
evidence.explanation: A review of all mutation-proven patients reports short stature as consistently present.

evidence.snippet: Characteristics shared by all twenty-three children included Hispanic descent, residence in Puerto Rico, bilateral dislocation of the hip, dislocated radial heads, short stature, and other osseous anomalies.
evidence.explanation: Short stature was shared by all twenty-three children in the original series.

steps/12.description: Short stature is one of the two features found in essentially every reported patient.

evidence.snippet: Characteristics shared by all twenty-three children included Hispanic descent, residence in Puerto Rico, bilateral dislocation of the hip, dislocated radial heads, short stature, and other osseous anomalies.
evidence.explanation: Bilateral hip dislocation was present in every child of the defining series.

evidence.snippet: Steel syndrome (STLS) encompasses characteristic facies, dwarfness, irreducible bilateral hip and radial head dislocation, and carpal bone coalition due to COL27A1 mutations.
evidence.explanation: Records that the bilateral hip dislocation of Steel syndrome is characteristically irreducible.

steps/13.description: Bilateral congenital dislocation of the hips, characteristically irreducible, is the presenting feature. Acetabular dysplasia and under-ossified capital femoral epiphyses accompany it.

evidence.snippet: The patient is a 4-year-old boy born to non-consanguineous healthy parents, with dysmorphic facial features, absent hip ossification centres, external rotation of both feet, relatively short stature, mild skin syndactyly, short mid phalanges and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
evidence.explanation: Reports absent hip ossification centres in a molecularly confirmed patient.

evidence.snippet: radiographs of the lower extremities showed bilateral hip dislocations, poorly ossified femoral heads and shallow bilateral acetabula
evidence.explanation: Documents poorly ossified femoral heads in the gene-discovery family.

steps/14.description: The capital femoral epiphyses are under-ossified or their ossification centres are absent, contributing to the instability of the hip.

evidence.snippet: Of the forty-six elbows in the twenty-three children, thirty-three were dislocated, as seen clinically and radiographically; eight were normal, both clinically and radiographically; and there was dysplasia at the radiocapitellar articulation of the remaining five.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies radial head dislocation across the elbows of the original cohort.

steps/15.description: Dislocation of the radial heads, usually bilateral, restricts elbow extension and forearm rotation. In the original series thirty-three of forty-six elbows were dislocated and a further five showed radiocapitellar dysplasia.

evidence.snippet: Twenty of the twenty-three children were found to have carpal coalitions.
evidence.explanation: Establishes carpal coalition as a near-universal feature in the defining cohort.

evidence.snippet: Both had bilateral capitate and hamate bone coalitions
evidence.explanation: Identifies capitate-hamate coalition as the specific fusion in the gene-discovery siblings.

steps/16.description: Carpal coalition, most often capitate-hamate fusion, is a hallmark radiographic sign. Twenty of the twenty-three children in the original series had carpal coalitions.

evidence.snippet: We describe for the first time, cleft palate and delayed carpal bone ossification as features of Steel syndrome.
evidence.explanation: First report of delayed carpal ossification as a Steel syndrome feature.

steps/17.description: Delayed carpal bone ossification was described as a feature of Steel syndrome in a review that also added cleft palate to the phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Fourteen children had scoliosis, and five of them were managed with spinal arthrodesis and correction.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies scoliosis frequency and its surgical burden in the original cohort.

steps/18.description: Scoliosis affected fourteen of the twenty-three children in the original series, five of whom required spinal arthrodesis.

evidence.snippet: Eight patients had talipes cavus bilaterally, which was not treated.
evidence.explanation: Documents bilateral pes cavus in the original series.

steps/19.description: Bilateral talipes cavus was present in eight of the twenty-three children originally described and was not treated.

evidence.snippet: Steel syndrome is a rare disorder of the skeleton characterized by facial dysmorphism, short stature, carpal coalition, dislocated radial heads, bilateral hip dislocation and vertical talus.
evidence.explanation: Lists vertical talus among the defining skeletal features.

steps/20.description: Vertical talus has been reported among the defining skeletal features in molecularly confirmed non-Puerto Rican patients.

evidence.snippet: Three patients had an anomaly of the cervical spine, with one deformity causing symptoms and signs that were treated with decompression.
evidence.explanation: Documents symptomatic cervical spine anomaly in the original cohort.

evidence.snippet: The cervical spine was significant for odontoid hypoplasia.
evidence.explanation: Odontoid hypoplasia in the proband of the gene-discovery family.

steps/21.description: Cervical spine anomalies, including odontoid hypoplasia, occur and can be symptomatic. One child in the original series required decompression.

evidence.snippet: An 11-year-old Korean boy presented with short stature, hip dysplasia, radial head dislocation, carpal coalition, genu valgum, and fixed patellar dislocation and was clinically diagnosed with Steel syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Reports genu valgum in a molecularly confirmed patient.

steps/22.description: Knee deformity, including genu valgum and fixed patellar dislocation, has been reported.

evidence.snippet: An 11-year-old Korean boy presented with short stature, hip dysplasia, radial head dislocation, carpal coalition, genu valgum, and fixed patellar dislocation and was clinically diagnosed with Steel syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Reports fixed patellar dislocation in a molecularly confirmed patient.

steps/23.description: Fixed patellar dislocation was described in a molecularly confirmed Korean patient.

evidence.snippet: Oval-shaped face with prominent forehead and mild frontal bossing and broad nasal bridge in both patients.
evidence.explanation: Describes the facial gestalt in the two siblings of the gene-discovery family.

steps/24.description: A long oval face with a prominent forehead and mild frontal bossing is part of the characteristic facial gestalt.

evidence.snippet: Oval-shaped face with prominent forehead and mild frontal bossing and broad nasal bridge in both patients.
evidence.explanation: Documents the broad nasal bridge in the gene-discovery family.

steps/25.description: A broad nasal bridge accompanies the long oval face and prominent forehead.

evidence.snippet: Physical examination revealed prominent forehead, hypertelorism, broad nasal bridge, midface hypoplasia with mild prognathism, pectus excavatum, short hands, genu valgum, and fixed patellar dislocation on the right side
evidence.explanation: Records hypertelorism in a molecularly confirmed patient.

steps/26.description: Hypertelorism was among the dysmorphic features recorded when the original patients were re-evaluated, and it recurs in molecularly confirmed patients.

evidence.snippet: showed short stature (<5%), mild midface hypoplasia with slightly anteverted nares, bilateral fifth finger clinodactyly, decreased adduction of the hips bilaterally
evidence.explanation: Documents midface hypoplasia on follow-up of the gene-discovery siblings.

steps/27.description: Mild midface hypoplasia, sometimes with slightly anteverted nares, is part of the facial phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Follow-up examinations of patients II-1 and II-2 at 14 and 12 years of age, respectively, showed short stature (<5%), mild midface hypoplasia with slightly anteverted nares, bilateral fifth finger clinodactyly, decreased adduction of the hips bilaterally andpes planus.
evidence.explanation: Records bilateral fifth finger clinodactyly in the gene-discovery siblings.

evidence.snippet: Other features include dislocated radial heads, scoliosis, lordosis, carpal coalition, facial dysmorphism, hearing loss, bilateral fifth finger clinodactyly, knee deformities and developmental delay.
evidence.explanation: Confirms fifth finger clinodactyly across the mutation-proven cohort.

steps/28.description: Bilateral fifth finger clinodactyly is a recurrent minor limb anomaly.

evidence.snippet: In addition, the affected child had severe non-progressive sensorineural hearing loss not reported previously.
evidence.explanation: First report extending the Steel syndrome phenotype to sensorineural hearing loss.

evidence.snippet: all three affected individuals presented with bilateral hearing loss with onset after 30 years of age
evidence.explanation: Shows adult-onset hearing loss in founder-allele homozygotes, an age-dependent presentation.

steps/29.description: Sensorineural hearing loss is not part of the original Puerto Rican description but is common in patients with severe or loss-of-function COL27A1 alleles, in whom it is congenital; in founder-allele homozygotes it appears in adult life.

evidence.snippet: The two additional variants reported here are predicted to introduce frameshift or splice changes that result in the introduction of early termination codons that lead to nonsense mediated processing and clearance of the mutant transcripts, effectively resulting in loss-of-function (LoF) alleles with consequent loss of the COL27A1 protein.
evidence.explanation: States the step from null COL27A1 alleles to loss of the protein product.

edges/2.description: Missense glycine substitutions in the triple helix yield a misfolded protein, while frameshift and splice alleles introduce premature termination codons whose transcripts are cleared, so both classes converge on a deficit of functional collagen XXVII.

evidence.snippet: Collagen XXVII plays an important structural role in the pericellular extracellular matrix of the growth plate and is required for the organisation of the proliferative zone.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that mutant collagen XXVII acts by disorganising the growth-plate pericellular matrix.

edges/3.description: Collagen XXVII normally accumulates in the pericellular matrix around growth-plate chondrocytes, so its structural disruption or absence is directly a defect of that matrix.

evidence.snippet: Mouse Col27a1 was found to be expressed in the cartilaginous structures associated with inner ear development and cochlear epithelium
evidence.explanation: Establishes the inner-ear expression domain that makes the cartilage there subject to the same collagen deficit.

edges/4.description: The same collagen deficit applies wherever the protein is normally deposited, and the gene is expressed in the cartilaginous structures of the developing inner ear. This is the branch point at which the auditory arm of the phenotype separates from the growth-plate arm.

evidence.snippet: However abnormal or absent collagen XXVII protein in the ECM results in collapse of the proliferative zone and disorganization of the cartilaginous zones of the growth plate preventing normal endochondral bone growth
evidence.explanation: States the causal step from abnormal matrix collagen XXVII to proliferative-zone collapse.

edges/5.description: The pericellular matrix is the scaffold that lets proliferative chondrocytes flatten and stack into columns; when it is disorganised, that architecture fails.

evidence.snippet: However abnormal or absent collagen XXVII protein in the ECM results in collapse of the proliferative zone and disorganization of the cartilaginous zones of the growth plate preventing normal endochondral bone growth
evidence.explanation: Names proliferative-zone collapse as what prevents normal endochondral bone growth.

edges/6.description: Columnar proliferative chondrocytes drive longitudinal growth, so their loss prevents normal endochondral bone growth.

evidence.snippet: We modeled the orthologous variant in murine Col27a1 and found it recapitulates some of the major Steel syndrome associated skeletal features including reduced body length, scoliosis, and a more rounded skull shape.
evidence.explanation: The knock-in of the human allele reproduces reduced body length, linking the growth-plate lesion to short stature.

evidence.snippet: We modeled the orthologous variant in murine Col27a1 and found it recapitulates some of the major Steel syndrome associated skeletal features including reduced body length, scoliosis, and a more rounded skull shape.

genes/0.notes: COL27A1 lies on chromosome 9q32, spans 61 exons and encodes a 1860-amino-acid pro-peptide of fibrillar collagen type XXVII. The Puerto Rican founder allele c.2089G>C p.(Gly697Arg) replaces a conserved glycine of the Gly-Xaa-Yaa repeat in the triple-helical domain and behaves as a hypomorph; carriers are phenotypically normal. Reported non-founder alleles include missense (p.Gly802Glu, p.Gly841Arg, p.Gly850Arg, p.Gly676Arg, p.Ala99Thr, p.Pro1019His), frameshift, nonsense, splice-site and multi-exon deletion variants.

treatments/0.description: Operative reduction of the dislocated hips has an unfavourable record in Steel syndrome. In the original series every hip treated by reduction augmented by an operation redislocated, and among closed reductions the results were satisfactory only in patients still skeletally immature at review. Untreated hips functioned satisfactorily over the reported follow-up. This history is why surgical reduction is approached cautiously rather than as routine.

open_questions/0.rationale: Both published mouse models, the engineered 87-amino-acid deletion and the knock-in of the human founder allele, kill most homozygotes perinatally through a lung defect or presumed respiratory insufficiency. Human patients carrying frameshift, nonsense and splice alleles that abolish the protein are viable and are not reported to have respiratory problems. The growth-plate readouts from these mice are the main mechanistic evidence in this entry, so the weight they can carry depends on whether the murine dependence on collagen XXVII in lung is a species-specific requirement or a difference in residual protein.

treatments/0.description: Anticonvulsant treatment is symptom-directed management for SSADH-associated epileptic seizures rather than a proven correction of the enzyme defect; vigabatrin and tiagabine are generally avoided because they can further elevate GABA signaling.

evidence.snippet: Treatment was mainly aimed to control epileptic seizures and psychiatric symptoms.
evidence.explanation: Long-term registry cohort supports supportive management of psychiatric symptoms.

evidence.snippet: Despite ambitious scientific effort, detailed knowledge about many aspects of the pathophysiology of the underlying enzyme defect is still lacking, and at present, no curative treatment that would directly target the enzyme deficiency is available for SSADH-D.
evidence.explanation: Review evidence supports limiting current treatment claims to symptomatic/supportive care.

treatments/1.description: Current management includes supportive treatment for psychiatric and behavioral symptoms, with no approved curative therapy for the underlying SSADH enzyme deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Patients with temporal lobe epilepsy showed a significantly larger exponent, corresponding to inhibition-directed E/I balance, in bilateral frontal and temporal regions.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports altered excitation/inhibition balance in temporal lobe epilepsy at the network level.

evidence.snippet: Limited to patients with temporal lobe epilepsy, we detected a significant correlation between the exponent and the cortical expression of GABRA1, GRIN2A, GABRD, GABRG2, KCNA2 and PDYN genes.
evidence.explanation: Supports molecular correlates of altered excitation/inhibition balance in temporal lobe epilepsy.

steps/0.description: Temporal lobe epilepsy is associated with altered excitation/inhibition balance across temporal and connected cortical regions, with molecular correlates implicating both GABAergic and glutamatergic signaling.

evidence.snippet: Our results give insight into vulnerable neural networks in pediatric focal epilepsy and suggest thalamocortical pathway damage as a potential mechanism of executive function impairment in temporal lobe epilepsy but not frontal lobe epilepsy.
evidence.explanation: Supports a distributed thalamocortical circuit mechanism for cognitive dysfunction in temporal lobe epilepsy, though this evidence is specific to a pediatric cohort.

steps/1.description: Vulnerable thalamocortical pathways can contribute to cognitive dysfunction in temporal lobe epilepsy, indicating that the disorder affects distributed neural circuits beyond the temporal focus itself.

evidence.snippet: Initial management of patients with temporal lobe epilepsy is with antiepileptic drugs, but these control seizures in only half the patients.
evidence.explanation: Supports antiseizure medication therapy as first-line management in TLE, while also showing that medication failure is common.

evidence.snippet: All approved ASMs were effective as add-on treatment for focal epilepsy.
evidence.explanation: Supports ongoing pharmacotherapy in TLE because TLE is a focal epilepsy syndrome, although the evidence is not specific to TLE alone.

treatments/0.description: Initial management of temporal lobe epilepsy is pharmacotherapy using antiseizure medications used across focal epilepsies, although many patients do not achieve durable seizure freedom and later meet criteria for drug-resistant disease.

evidence.snippet: At one year, the cumulative proportion of patients who were free of seizures impairing awareness was 58 percent in the surgical group and 8 percent in the medical group (P<0.001).
evidence.explanation: Supports surgical treatment as an effective option for carefully selected patients with drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy.

treatments/1.description: In carefully selected patients with drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy, surgical treatment offers substantially higher rates of seizure freedom than continued medical therapy and remains a key escalation path once pharmacoresistance is established.

evidence.snippet: NRAS was the most common mutation (33.9%), followed by TERT (22.6%), DICER1 (15.5%), HRAS (11.9%), and PTEN (10.7%).

steps/7.description: TERT promoter mutation is a secondary, progression-associated somatic event rather than a truncal driver. It is the second most frequently mutated gene in follicular thyroid carcinoma and is associated with distant metastasis, advanced stage, recurrence and disease-specific mortality. It is entered here as a separate progression arm converging on distant metastasis, because the published evidence links the mutation to metastatic outcome rather than placing it in the truncal RAS/PAX8-PPARG sequence.

evidence.snippet: In 134 samples, genetic tests for N/H/KRAS and TERT promoter mutations and PAX8/PPARγ rearrangement were performed.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that RAS-family mutations and PAX8/PPARG rearrangement are the recurrent driver alterations assayed in a large follicular thyroid carcinoma cohort.

evidence.snippet: NRAS was the most common mutation (33.9%), followed by TERT (22.6%), DICER1 (15.5%), HRAS (11.9%), and PTEN (10.7%).
evidence.explanation: Gives the per-gene somatic mutation frequencies in 168 follicular thyroid carcinoma samples, establishing NRAS and HRAS as recurrently mutated rather than merely assayed.

evidence.snippet: NRAS mutations were more frequent in metastatic tumors (42.4%) than primary tumors (29.2%).
evidence.explanation: Shows the NRAS driver is enriched in metastatic relative to primary tumours in the same cohort.

steps/8.description: Early oncogenic events in follicular thyroid carcinoma are dominated by activating point mutations in the RAS family (NRAS, HRAS, KRAS) and by the PAX8-PPARG gene fusion arising from a t(2;3)(q13;p25) translocation. These truncal alterations occur in thyroid follicular cells and define the "RAS-like" molecular class of follicular-patterned thyroid tumors. Mutant RAS is locked in the active GTP-bound state, and the chimeric PAX8-PPARG protein exhibits neomorphic transcriptional activity dysregulating differentiation and metabolism.

evidence.snippet: Genetic rearrangements in TCDFC (RET/PTC, PAX8/PPARG) and mutations in RAS, BRAF, TERT promoter (TERTp), TP53, PIK3CA, and AKT1 are discussed.
evidence.explanation: Supports the convergence of RAS, PAX8/PPARG, PIK3CA, and AKT1 alterations onto MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling in follicular-cell-derived thyroid carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: NRAS was the most common mutation (33.9%), followed by TERT (22.6%), DICER1 (15.5%), HRAS (11.9%), and PTEN (10.7%).
evidence.explanation: Establishes PTEN as a recurrently mutated gene in follicular thyroid carcinoma, at 10.7% of 168 samples.

evidence.snippet: In a healthy cell, PTEN dephosphorylates Akt to maintain proper signaling balance; however, loss-of-function mutations in PTEN, which we observed in over 10% of samples
evidence.explanation: Ties loss-of-function PTEN variants in this cohort to unchecked AKT activation, which is the PI3K/AKT arm of this node.

steps/9.description: RAS-family mutations and PI3K-pathway lesions co-activate the MAPK (RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK) and PI3K/AKT cascades. In follicular thyroid carcinoma the PI3K/AKT arm is especially prominent, promoting cell growth, survival, metabolism, and invasive behavior, while moderate "RAS-like" MAPK output is associated with the follicular architecture.

evidence.snippet: The cytoarchitectural features of FTC are similar to those of follicular adenoma (FA), and it is difficult to preoperatively distinguish between FA and FTC.
evidence.explanation: Supports that follicular thyroid carcinoma forms a follicular-patterned proliferation cytoarchitecturally resembling the benign follicular adenoma.

steps/10.description: Persistent MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling promotes uncontrolled proliferation of transformed thyroid follicular cells, producing an encapsulated follicular-patterned neoplasm.

evidence.snippet: Though follicular thyroid carcinoma can be confirmed postoperatively by the histological findings of capsular or vascular invasion
evidence.explanation: Supports capsular or vascular invasion as the defining histopathologic criterion for follicular thyroid carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: FTCs are classified as minimally invasive, encapsulated angioinvasive, and widely invasive FTCs.
evidence.explanation: Supports the invasion-based histopathologic subclassification of follicular thyroid carcinoma.

steps/11.description: Capsular and/or vascular invasion is the histopathologic hallmark that defines follicular thyroid carcinoma and distinguishes it from the benign follicular adenoma. The degree of vascular invasion (minimally invasive, encapsulated angioinvasive, widely invasive) is a key prognostic determinant.

evidence.snippet: Follicular thyroid carcinoma usually metastasizes through a hematogenous route, the most frequent sites of distant metastases are bone and lung
evidence.explanation: Supports hematogenous dissemination to bone and lung as the characteristic metastatic pattern of follicular thyroid carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: thyroid follicular carcinomas are mostly observed in hematogenous metastases
evidence.explanation: Supports the predominance of hematogenous (rather than lymphatic) metastasis in follicular thyroid carcinoma.

steps/12.description: Following vascular invasion, follicular thyroid carcinoma disseminates predominantly through the bloodstream rather than via lymphatics, with the most frequent distant metastatic sites being bone and lung. This hematogenous pattern distinguishes follicular carcinoma from the lymphatically spreading papillary carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: The cytoarchitectural features of FTC are similar to those of follicular adenoma (FA), and it is difficult to preoperatively distinguish between FA and FTC.
evidence.explanation: Supports that follicular thyroid carcinoma presents as a follicular thyroid nodule that is difficult to distinguish preoperatively from a benign adenoma.

steps/13.description: Follicular thyroid carcinoma typically presents as a solitary thyroid nodule, often discovered on physical examination or incidentally on imaging.

evidence.snippet: the most frequent sites of distant metastases are bone and lung
evidence.explanation: Supports bone as a frequent distant metastatic site, the basis for metastatic bone pain in follicular thyroid carcinoma.

steps/14.description: Hematogenous metastasis to bone can cause bone pain and skeletal morbidity in advanced or widely invasive follicular thyroid carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: the most frequent sites of distant metastases are bone and lung
evidence.explanation: Supports lung as a frequent distant metastatic site, the basis for respiratory symptoms in metastatic follicular thyroid carcinoma.

steps/15.description: Pulmonary metastases from hematogenous spread can produce respiratory symptoms including dyspnea in advanced follicular thyroid carcinoma.

edges/8.description: Sustained mitogenic signaling drives clonal expansion of transformed follicular cells.

evidence.snippet: patients typically present with a solitary thyroid nodule
evidence.explanation: States the clinical presentation of follicular thyroid carcinoma as a solitary nodule, the observable form of the proliferation at this node.

edges/9.description: The follicular-patterned proliferation is what presents clinically as a solitary thyroid nodule.

edges/10.description: The proliferating follicular neoplasm breaches its capsule and invades vessels, the defining malignant feature that separates carcinoma from adenoma.

edges/11.description: Vascular invasion provides the route for hematogenous dissemination to distant organs, particularly bone and lung.

evidence.snippet: due to its independent association with distant metastases and increased disease-specific mortality
evidence.explanation: Penna et al. attribute the prognostic value of TERT promoter mutation to its independent association with distant metastases.

edges/12.description: TERT promoter mutation is associated with distant metastatic disease; the steps between the promoter mutation and dissemination are not established, so the edge is recorded as indirect.

evidence.snippet: the most frequent sites of distant metastases are bone and lung

edges/13.description: Skeletal metastatic deposits produce bone pain.

evidence.snippet: In 134 samples, genetic tests for N/H/KRAS and TERT promoter mutations and PAX8/PPARγ rearrangement were performed.

genes/1.notes: HRAS is among the RAS-family genes (N/H/KRAS) assayed and recurrently altered in follicular thyroid carcinoma, contributing to the "RAS-like" molecular class.

evidence.snippet: In 134 samples, genetic tests for N/H/KRAS and TERT promoter mutations and PAX8/PPARγ rearrangement were performed.
evidence.explanation: Supports KRAS as one of the RAS-family genes (N/H/KRAS) tested as a recurrent driver in follicular thyroid carcinoma.

genes/2.notes: KRAS is among the RAS-family genes (N/H/KRAS) recurrently mutated in follicular thyroid carcinoma and part of the RAS-like driver class.

evidence.snippet: In 134 samples, genetic tests for N/H/KRAS and TERT promoter mutations and PAX8/PPARγ rearrangement were performed.
evidence.explanation: Supports PAX8/PPARG rearrangement as a recurrent driver alteration tested in follicular thyroid carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: In 134 samples, genetic tests for N/H/KRAS and TERT promoter mutations and PAX8/PPARγ rearrangement were performed.
evidence.explanation: Supports PAX8 as a fusion partner in the recurrent PAX8/PPARG rearrangement of follicular thyroid carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: Genetic rearrangements in TCDFC (RET/PTC, PAX8/PPARG) and mutations in RAS, BRAF, TERT promoter (TERTp), TP53, PIK3CA, and AKT1 are discussed.
evidence.explanation: Supports PI3K/AKT-pathway alterations (PIK3CA, AKT1; PTEN loss derepresses the same axis) as contributors to follicular-cell-derived thyroid carcinoma.

genes/5.notes: Loss of PTEN phosphatase function results in unopposed PI3K/AKT signaling and is a driver of follicular thyroid carcinoma; germline PTEN mutations underlie Cowden syndrome, which predisposes to follicular thyroid carcinoma. PTEN is one of the PIK3CA/AKT/PTEN-axis alterations driving PI3K pathway activation.

evidence.snippet: TERT promoter mutations were associated with distant metastasis, advanced TNM stage, recurrence and disease-specific mortality.
evidence.explanation: Supports TERT promoter mutation as a progression-associated marker of adverse outcome in follicular thyroid carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: TERTp mutations can serve as a marker of more aggressive disease in all the subtypes of thyroid carcinoma, being the best current marker of poor prognosis
evidence.explanation: Supports TERT promoter mutation as the strongest current prognostic marker across thyroid carcinoma subtypes including follicular carcinoma.

genes/6.notes: TERT promoter mutations are progression events that activate telomerase and are the best current marker of poor prognosis in thyroid carcinoma. In FTC they are associated with distant metastasis, advanced stage, recurrence, and disease-specific mortality, especially when coexisting with RAS mutation.

evidence.snippet: The goals of initial surgical therapy for patients with FTC are to improve overall and disease-specific survival, reduce the risk of persistent/recurrent disease and associated morbidity
evidence.explanation: Supports surgery as the mainstay of initial therapy for follicular thyroid carcinoma.

treatments/0.description: Surgical resection is the mainstay of initial therapy for follicular thyroid carcinoma, aiming to improve survival, reduce recurrence, and permit accurate staging and risk stratification.

evidence.snippet: Recurrence and distant metastasis of FTC are treated with radioactive iodine (RAI).
evidence.explanation: Supports radioactive iodine as therapy for recurrent and metastatic follicular thyroid carcinoma.

treatments/1.description: Radioactive iodine (RAI) is used to treat recurrence and distant metastasis of differentiated follicular thyroid carcinoma, exploiting iodine uptake by differentiated follicular tumor cells. Some tumors become RAI-refractory with dedifferentiation.

treatments/2.description: Levothyroxine is given after thyroidectomy both as hormone replacement and to suppress TSH, removing a growth stimulus to any residual differentiated thyroid tumor cells.

evidence.snippet: Multi-tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sorafenib and lenvatinib are utilized for treating RAI-refractory FTCs.
evidence.explanation: Supports multikinase inhibitors (sorafenib, lenvatinib) for radioiodine-refractory follicular thyroid carcinoma.

treatments/3.description: Multi-tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sorafenib and lenvatinib are used for radioactive-iodine-refractory follicular thyroid carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: patients aged 16 years and older with radioiodine-refractory DTC (papillary or follicular and their variants)
evidence.explanation: Confirms follicular carcinoma and its variants were an eligible histology in COSMIC-311, so the trial result applies to this entry and not only to the papillary sibling.

evidence.snippet: cabozantinib showed significant improvement in progression-free survival over placebo: median not reached ... versus 1·9 months (1·8-3·6); hazard ratio 0·22 (96% CI 0·13-0·36; p<0·0001)
evidence.explanation: Reports the randomised progression-free survival benefit supporting cabozantinib after failure of the multikinase inhibitors curated above.

evidence.snippet: Grade 3 or 4 adverse events occurred in 71 (57%) of 125 patients receiving cabozantinib and 16 (26%) of 62 receiving placebo
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the grade 3-4 toxicity burden stated in the description, so the efficacy claim is not curated without its safety cost.

evidence.snippet: Cabozantinib contributed high-certainty evidence for progression-free survival in radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer after previous VEGFR-targeted therapy
evidence.explanation: GRADE certainty rating from a 2026 systematic review of treatment-resistant malignancies, corroborating (not solely supporting) the COSMIC-311 result above. Non-peer-reviewed preprint; cited only alongside the peer-reviewed trial report.

treatments/4.description: Cabozantinib is a multi-kinase inhibitor (VEGFR2, MET, AXL, RET) used after progression on lenvatinib or sorafenib in radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer. The randomised placebo-controlled COSMIC-311 trial enrolled radioiodine-refractory papillary *and* follicular carcinoma (and their variants) and met its progression-free survival endpoint at interim analysis, at the cost of substantially more grade 3-4 toxicity.

evidence.snippet: Eight of the nine altered amino acids are conserved and lie either within a domain essential for binding interacting proteins or in the C-terminal RING finger catalytic domain.
evidence.explanation: Localizes the disease variants to the two functional hotspots.

evidence.snippet: TOKAS is caused exclusively by variants in the gene encoding the E3 ubiquitin ligase gene RLIM, also known as RNF12.
evidence.explanation: States RLIM as the sole known causal gene.

steps/1.description: A germline missense variant in X-linked RLIM, present in hemizygous state in affected males, alters a conserved residue in the basic regulatory region or the RING catalytic domain.

evidence.snippet: RLIM p.(Tyr421Cys) is correctly localised to the nucleus, but is readily degraded by the proteasome.
evidence.explanation: Direct demonstration of variant protein instability in an embryonic stem cell model.

steps/2.description: The basic-region-adjacent variant p.Tyr421Cys is correctly localized to the nucleus but is rapidly degraded by the proteasome, lowering RLIM protein abundance. Whether other TOKAS variants act partly through instability is not known.

evidence.snippet: In vivo experiments in rlim mutant zebrafish showed that wild type RLIM rescued the zebrafish rlim phenotype, whereas the patient-specific missense RLIM variants failed to rescue the phenotype and thus represent likely severe loss-of-function mutations.
evidence.explanation: In vivo evidence that patient alleles lack RLIM function.

evidence.snippet: The RLIM p.(Tyr421Cys) variant also displays significantly impaired E3 ubiquitin ligase activity, which interferes with RLIM function in Xist long-non-coding RNA induction that initiates imprinted X-chromosome inactivation.
evidence.explanation: A basic-region-adjacent variant also impairs ligase activity.

steps/3.description: Reduced RING E3 ligase activity of RLIM is the shared molecular consequence of the TOKAS variants that have been tested, and the zebrafish rescue experiments indicate the variants behave as severe loss-of-function alleles.

evidence.snippet: RNF12 causes ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of REX1, and Rnf12 knockout embryonic stem cells show an increased level of REX1.
evidence.explanation: Establishes REX1 as a degradative substrate whose levels rise without RLIM.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, RNF12 chromatin targeting is critical for REX1 ubiquitylation and downstream RNF12-dependent gene regulation.
evidence.explanation: Links the basic-region chromatin recruitment function to REX1 ubiquitylation.

evidence.snippet: Our data demonstrate that RLIM-specific flow cytometry reporters based on either the full length or a degron region of the substrate REX1 measure RLIM activity in cells.
evidence.explanation: REX1 degradation is used as the cellular readout of RLIM activity for variant assessment.

steps/4.description: REX1 (ZFP42), a pluripotency-associated transcriptional repressor, is the principal RLIM substrate. RLIM targets it for proteasomal degradation; RLIM loss raises REX1 levels in embryonic stem cells. RLIM reaches REX1 at gene promoters through chromatin recruitment via its basic region.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, this RNF12-USP26 axis was disrupted by RLIM and USP26 variants found in TOKAS and infertility patients, respectively.
evidence.explanation: TOKAS variants disrupt the RLIM-USP26 axis.

evidence.snippet: RNF12 relieved REX1-mediated repression of Usp26, leading to an increase in USP26 abundance and the formation of RNF12-USP26 complexes.
evidence.explanation: Places the USP26 loop downstream of REX1 degradation.

steps/5.description: In mouse embryonic stem cells and testis, RLIM relieves REX1 repression of the deubiquitylase USP26, which in turn stabilizes RLIM, forming a feed-forward loop required for germ cell differentiation in vitro. TOKAS variants disrupt this loop; its relevance to the human phenotype, for example to hypogenitalism, has not been tested.

evidence.snippet: RNF12 specifically binds to Smad7 and induces its polyubiquitination and degradation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes SMAD7 as a degradative RLIM substrate.

steps/6.description: RLIM binds and polyubiquitylates the inhibitory SMAD7, targeting it for degradation. RLIM-deficient mouse embryonic stem cells accumulate SMAD7.

evidence.snippet: Depletion of RNF12 dramatically reduced TGF-β/Smad-induced effects in mammalian cells, whereas ectopic expression of RNF12 strongly enhanced these responses.
evidence.explanation: RLIM depletion reduces TGF-beta pathway output.

steps/7.description: Excess SMAD7 dampens TGF-beta family signaling. In RLIM-deficient embryonic stem cells this relieves BMP-mediated repression of neural induction and reduces activin-induced anterior mesoderm formation. Whether this operates in TOKAS patient tissues is not shown.

evidence.snippet: Here we show, by targeting a conditional knockout of Rnf12 to oocytes where RLIM accumulates to high levels, that the maternal transmission of the mutant X chromosome (Δm) leads to lethality in female embryos as a result of defective imprinted XCI.
evidence.explanation: RLIM is required for imprinted X-inactivation in mice.

evidence.snippet: Genetic ablation of Rex1 in Rnf12-/- mice rescues the Rnf12-/- iXCI phenotype, and results in viable and fertile Rnf12-/-:Rex1-/- female mice displaying normal iXCI and rXCI.
evidence.explanation: REX1 is the substrate through which RLIM controls imprinted X-inactivation.

evidence.snippet: Initiation of XCI is markedly reduced in differentiating female heterozygous Rnf12(+/-) ES cells.
evidence.explanation: Reduced RLIM dosage reduces initiation of X-inactivation in embryonic stem cells.

evidence.snippet: These results provide evidence that RLIM is dispensable for rXCI, indicating that in mice an RLIM-independent mechanism activates Xist in the embryo proper.
evidence.explanation: Refutes an obligatory role for RLIM in random X-inactivation of the embryo proper, limiting this node to imprinted X-inactivation.

steps/8.description: In mice, maternally deposited RLIM is required to induce Xist and initiate imprinted X-chromosome inactivation, and REX1 is its critical target; RLIM is dispensable for random X-inactivation in the epiblast. Because affected patients are hemizygous males, the contribution of this mechanism to the human male phenotype is unclear; it may bear on carrier females and on the skewed X-inactivation they show.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show that RNF12/Rlim mutation in male ESCs accelerates induction of neural lineage markers and establishment of neurite outgrowths, a phenotype associated with ID.
evidence.explanation: Direct cell-model evidence of accelerated neural differentiation.

evidence.snippet: We show that RNF12 catalytic activity is required for proper stem cell maintenance and neural differentiation, and this is disrupted by patient-associated XLID mutation.
evidence.explanation: Patient variants disrupt the stem cell maintenance and neural differentiation functions.

steps/9.description: Male embryonic stem cells lacking RLIM, or carrying patient variants, show premature induction of neural lineage markers and early neurite outgrowth, a pattern the authors relate to intellectual disability. The link to the human brain phenotype is inferred from this cell model.

evidence.snippet: A total of 40 affected males have X-linked intellectual disability (XLID) and variable behavioral anomalies with or without congenital malformations.

evidence.snippet: A recent cohort study showed that males with TOKAS present with intellectual disability (100% cases, mild to severe), visceral abnormalities including differences of sexual development (DSD, including micropenis, hypospadias or testicular hypoplasia; 90%), congenital diaphragmatic hernias (CDHs) (50%), congenital heart disease (17%), omphalocele (10%), cleft palate (8%), polysplenia (5%) and intestinal malrotation (5%).

evidence.snippet: Postmortem examination revealed congenital diaphragmatic hernia with aplasia of the posterolateral left hemi-diaphragm, displacement of the mediastinum to the right, herniation of the small and large intestine, stomach, spleen, left lobe of liver, and pancreas into the left hemithorax, absent middle lobe right lung and severe bilateral pulmonary hypoplasia.

evidence.explanation: In the same study, basic-region variants still ubiquitylated REX1 in cells, so the REX1 defect is not shown for every variant class.

evidence.snippet: We show that RNF12/RLIM XLID mutants display impaired ubiquitylation of the key developmental RNF12 substrates REX1 and SMAD7.

evidence.snippet: The RLIM p.(Tyr421Cys) variant also displays significantly impaired E3 ubiquitin ligase activity, which interferes with RLIM function in Xist long-non-coding RNA induction that initiates imprinted X-chromosome inactivation.

evidence.snippet: Smad7 levels were increased in RNF12-deficient mouse embryonic stem cells, resulting in mitigation of both BMP-mediated repression of neural induction and activin-induced anterior mesoderm formation.

evidence.snippet: Altogether, these results map out a pathway whereby RNF12/RLIM mutations in XLID patients disrupt E3 ubiquitin ligase activity, leading to abnormal stem cell behavior and accelerated neural development characteristic of ID.
evidence.explanation: The authors propose accelerated neural development as the route to intellectual disability; this is an inference from a cell model.

evidence.snippet: Postmortem examination revealed congenital diaphragmatic hernia with aplasia of the posterolateral left hemi-diaphragm, displacement of the mediastinum to the right, herniation of the small and large intestine, stomach, spleen, left lobe of liver, and pancreas into the left hemithorax, absent middle lobe right lung and severe bilateral pulmonary hypoplasia.
evidence.explanation: Autopsy of a TOKAS neonate showing CDH with herniated viscera and severe pulmonary hypoplasia.

evidence.snippet: All RLIM variants identified are missense changes co-segregating with the phenotype and predicted to affect protein function.
evidence.explanation: Co-segregation of RLIM missense variants with disease across nine families.

evidence.snippet: In 19 families, we detected likely causative protein truncating and missense variants in 7 novel and validated XLID genes (CLCN4, CNKSR2, FRMPD4, KLHL15, LAS1L, RLIM and USP27X)
evidence.explanation: Independent identification of RLIM as an X-linked intellectual disability gene in an X-exome screen.

evidence.snippet: No truncating variants have been reported and RLIM is predicted to be highly intolerant to loss-of-function variants
evidence.explanation: Supports the statement that the allelic spectrum is missense-only and that RLIM is loss-of-function intolerant.

evidence.snippet: This case highlights the essential role of multidisciplinary collaboration, including maternal-fetal medicine, genetics, neonatology, pathology, and palliative care, in providing coordinated, compassionate, and family-centered care in the setting of a life-limiting fetal diagnosis.
evidence.explanation: Case report describing multidisciplinary perinatal palliative care.

treatments/0.description: There is no disease-specific therapy. For antenatally diagnosed severe forms, care is coordinated across maternal-fetal medicine, genetics, neonatology, pathology and palliative care.

evidence.snippet: Once a maternally inherited RLIM pathogenic variant is identified, recurrence risk counseling becomes essential.
evidence.explanation: Recommends recurrence-risk counseling for families.

evidence.snippet: This study will facilitate antenatal diagnosis of TOKAS and will enable these families to benefit from appropriate genetic counselling.
evidence.explanation: Antenatal recognition enables genetic counseling.

treatments/1.description: Recurrence-risk counseling and carrier testing of female relatives after a maternally inherited variant is identified; prenatal diagnosis is available in subsequent pregnancies.

evidence.snippet: However, the relevant gene expression programmes that are disrupted to cause the syndromic features of TOKAS, such as diaphragmatic hernia, are yet to be elucidated.
evidence.explanation: The authors state the gap directly.

open_questions/0.rationale: The substrate-level defects (REX1, SMAD7) and the accelerated neural differentiation are shown only in mouse embryonic stem cells. No study has connected them to diaphragm, genital, heart or limb development. Only the diaphragmatic hernia, which PMID:33953269 names as a feature caused by disrupted RLIM function through unidentified programmes, carries a causal edge; the other malformations and the neurodevelopmental features are left without an upstream mechanism node rather than wired to one no source connects them to.

evidence.snippet: However, the lethality of this specific variant, and more generally the genotype-phenotype correlation in this syndrome, has not yet been explained.
evidence.explanation: States that the p.Arg611Cys severity is unexplained.

open_questions/1.rationale: Arg611 is the conserved linchpin arginine of the RING domain, which mediates E2 and ubiquitin interaction, but the reason for the severity of this variant relative to other ligase-impairing variants has not been explained.

evidence.snippet: Linkage of XLCM to the centromeric portion of the dystrophin or Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) locus at Xp21 was demonstrated with combined maximum logarithm of the scores of +4.33
evidence.explanation: Establishes DMD at Xp21 as the disease locus, the founding molecular evidence that XLDCM is a dystrophinopathy.

evidence.snippet: Abnormalities of cardiac dystrophin were shown by Western blotting with N-terminal dystrophin antibody, whereas skeletal muscle dystrophin was normal, suggesting primary involvement of the DMD gene with preferential involvement of cardiac muscle.
evidence.explanation: The heart-selective biochemical defect that defines the entity: abnormal cardiac dystrophin against normal skeletal-muscle dystrophin.

steps/1.description: The initiating lesion. The paradigmatic XLDCM mutation deletes the muscle (M) promoter and first muscle exon at the 5' end of DMD, abolishing transcription of the muscle dystrophin isoform (Dp427m); other XLDCM lesions include in-frame exon 45-55 deletions and destabilizing missense variants. Towbin's linkage study localized the disorder to the centromeric half of the dystrophin locus at Xp21 and showed that cardiac dystrophin was abnormal on Western blot while skeletal-muscle dystrophin was normal - the biochemical signature of a heart-preferential dystrophin defect.

evidence.snippet: the B isoform is well expressed in heart but confined to the atria. Since the B isoform can functionally replace the M isoform in the skeletal muscle, its expression in the heart could potentially exert the same rescue function.
evidence.explanation: The paper's own conclusion on the compensation-and-failure logic: the B isoform rescues skeletal muscle, but in the heart it is confined to the atria, so the ventricles have no replacement for the lost M isoform.

evidence.snippet: Unlike the M isoform, consistently detectable in all the heart regions, the B isoform was selectively expressed in atrial cardiomyocytes, but absent in ventricles and in conduction system structures.
evidence.explanation: The molecular-topography finding that grounds ventricular selectivity: no B isoform is available in the ventricle to replace the lost M isoform.

evidence.snippet: The ventricular dilatation seen in 5'-XLDC patients appears to be functionally related to loss of the M isoform, the only isoform transcribed in human ventricles
evidence.explanation: Ties the molecular finding to the clinical outcome (ventricular dilation) that the downstream chain models.

steps/2.description: The node on which the whole entry turns, and the reason XLDCM is cardiac-selective rather than a systemic dystrophinopathy. When the 5' mutation abolishes the muscle (M) dystrophin isoform, skeletal muscle compensates by up-regulating the brain (B) isoform from an intact downstream promoter. The ventricular myocardium cannot: in the healthy human heart the B isoform is expressed only in atrial cardiomyocytes and conduction tissue, and is absent from the ventricles, which transcribe the M isoform alone. With no compensatory transcript available, the ventricle is left dystrophin-deficient while the limbs are rescued.

evidence.snippet: Dystrophin connects the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix (ECM). Severing the link between the ECM and the intracellular cytoskeleton has a devastating impact on the homeostasis of skeletal muscle cells, leading to a range of muscular dystrophies. In addition, the loss of a functional DGC leads to progressive dilated cardiomyopathy and premature death.
evidence.explanation: States both the DGC's structural role and that losing it causes progressive dilated cardiomyopathy - the claim this node makes.

evidence.snippet: Localized to the sarcolemma, dystrophin is a major component of the dystrophin glycoprotein complex (DGC) along with the dystroglycan, sarcoglycan, and syntrophin/dystrobrevin complexes that link the cytoskeletal protein actin to the basal lamina of muscle fibers
evidence.explanation: Places dystrophin as the core DGC component at the sarcolemma, the structure this node loses.

steps/3.description: Dystrophin is the central member of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (DGC) at the sarcolemma, linking the intracellular actin cytoskeleton through dystroglycan and sarcoglycan subcomplexes to the extracellular matrix. Without dystrophin the DGC cannot assemble, and the mechanical and signaling link across the ventricular cardiomyocyte membrane is lost.

evidence.snippet: Dystrophin deficiency disrupts the DGC and causes the muscle membrane fragility and an increase in susceptibility to the mechanical stress, which leads to progressive muscle necrosis and degeneration in both skeletal and cardiac muscles
evidence.explanation: The membrane-fragility-under-mechanical-stress mechanism, stated for cardiac as well as skeletal muscle.

evidence.snippet: Dystrophin functions as a molecular spring and the DGC plays a critical role in maintaining the integrity of the sarcolemma.
evidence.explanation: The molecular-spring/membrane-integrity function whose loss produces contraction-induced injury.

steps/4.description: With the DGC gone, dystrophin can no longer act as the molecular spring that protects the membrane during contraction, so each cardiac cycle inflicts microtears on the ventricular cardiomyocyte sarcolemma. This is the primary cardiomyocyte insult that the maladaptive-remodeling module models generically; here it is driven specifically by the ventricular dystrophin deficit and is aggravated by mechanical loading (the "use hypothesis").

evidence.snippet: Sarcolemmal instability, leading to calcium mishandling and overload in the cardiac myocyte, is a key mechanistic contributor to muscle cell death, fibrosis, and diminished cardiac contractile function in DMD patients.
evidence.explanation: Places calcium overload as the link between sarcolemmal instability and the cell death, fibrosis and contractile failure of the downstream nodes.

steps/5.description: Sarcolemmal microdamage and disrupted mechanosensitive channel regulation admit excess calcium into the ventricular cardiomyocyte, and intracellular calcium handling becomes overwhelmed. Calcium overload activates calcium-dependent proteases and injures mitochondria, driving the cell-death programme downstream.

evidence.snippet: Dystrophin deficiency disrupts the DGC and causes the muscle membrane fragility and an increase in susceptibility to the mechanical stress, which leads to progressive muscle necrosis and degeneration in both skeletal and cardiac muscles
evidence.explanation: Names progressive necrosis and degeneration of cardiac muscle as the tissue-level consequence of the dystrophin deficit.

evidence.snippet: is a key mechanistic contributor to muscle cell death, fibrosis, and diminished cardiac contractile function in DMD patients.
evidence.explanation: Couples cell death with fibrosis and contractile decline, the transition this node makes to the heart-failure outcome.

steps/6.description: Chronic calcium overload and membrane injury cause cardiomyocyte necrosis, with secondary replacement fibrosis and fatty infiltration that characteristically begin in the left ventricular posterobasal/inferolateral wall - the territory that lights up as late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI across dystrophinopathy cardiomyopathy.

evidence.snippet: XLDCM is caused by mutations of the Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) gene and results in lethal heart failure in individuals between 10 and 20 years.
evidence.explanation: The heart-failure outcome and its characteristic age window in males.

evidence.snippet: X-linked cardiomyopathy (XLCM) is a rapidly progressive primary myocardial disorder presenting in teenage males as congestive heart failure.
evidence.explanation: The clinical presentation this node describes, from the original linkage cohort.

steps/7.description: The clinical endpoint: progressive left ventricular dilation with systolic dysfunction, presenting as congestive heart failure. In classic XLDCM this is rapid and lethal in adolescent and young-adult males; in the exon 45-55 subtype it is more indolent and more responsive to standard heart-failure therapy. The failing, fibrotic ventricle also provides the substrate for ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death.

evidence.snippet: showed rapidly progressive heart failure and ventricular arrhythmias between 10 and 20 years old.
evidence.explanation: Ventricular arrhythmia arising in the failing dystrophin-deficient ventricle of the founding XLDCM kindred.

steps/8.description: A fibrotic, dilated ventricle is electrically unstable: replacement fibrosis and myocyte loss create a re-entrant/ectopic substrate that generates ventricular arrhythmia, a major contributor to mortality in XLDCM.

evidence.snippet: The cause of death was certified as an early dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM)/dysfunction of the left ventricle secondary to DMD
evidence.explanation: A documented case of sudden death from dystrophin-deficient dilated cardiomyopathy, the terminal event this node models.

steps/9.description: Sudden cardiac death can be the presenting event, occurring without preceding overt heart failure - documented at autopsy by elevated pericardial-fluid NT-proBNP marking undiagnosed left ventricular dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: X-linked dilated cardiomyopathy (XLDCM) is a distinct phenotype of dystrophinopathy characterized by preferential cardiac involvement without any overt skeletal myopathy.
evidence.explanation: States both the defining cardiac phenotype and its isolation from skeletal disease.

steps/10.description: The defining and near-universal feature: left ventricular dilation with systolic dysfunction, in relative or complete isolation from skeletal myopathy.

evidence.snippet: X-linked cardiomyopathy (XLCM) is a rapidly progressive primary myocardial disorder presenting in teenage males as congestive heart failure.
evidence.explanation: Congestive heart failure as the presenting manifestation in teenage males.

steps/11.description: The usual presenting syndrome in affected males, typically in adolescence or the early twenties.

evidence.snippet: Absolute LVEF% values reduced in both groups ('active': 62.5% ± 5.6% to 53.8% ± 4.0%; 'placebo': 60.6% ± 4.9% to 50.4% ± 8.5%).
evidence.explanation: Documents the progressive fall in left ventricular ejection fraction over follow-up in dystrophin-deficient cardiomyopathy; measured in a DMD cohort and applied to XLDCM as the same dystrophin-deficient cardiomyopathy, hence INDIRECT.

steps/12.description: The core objective measure of systolic dysfunction, tracked serially and used to trigger and titrate heart-failure therapy.

evidence.snippet: showed rapidly progressive heart failure and ventricular arrhythmias between 10 and 20 years old.
evidence.explanation: Ventricular arrhythmia alongside heart failure in the affected males of the founding XLDCM kindred.

steps/13.description: Emerges as the ventricle dilates and fibroses; a major contributor to mortality and sudden death.

evidence.snippet: Here, we reported a case of 29-year-old man who died suddenly.
evidence.explanation: A documented sudden death from previously undiagnosed dystrophin-deficient cardiomyopathy.

steps/14.description: Can occur without preceding overt heart failure, sometimes as the presenting event.

evidence.snippet: Serum CPK levels were increased in 11 of 13 patients.
evidence.explanation: Creatine phosphokinase was elevated in most, but not all, dystrophin-defect DCM patients, consistent with a variable, non-discriminating CK.

steps/15.description: Serum creatine kinase is variable in XLDCM - it can be markedly elevated but is often normal, particularly with exon 45-55 deletions and in later-onset or female cases - so unlike in classic Duchenne, a normal CK does not exclude the diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: It is known that about 8% of carriers present with dilated cardiomyopathy, though it may vary from 0% to 16.7%, depending on if the carrier is classified as having DMD or BMD.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the carrier-female cardiomyopathy risk and its range across DMD/BMD carrier classes.

steps/16.description: Carrier females are not cardiac-silent. About 8% develop dilated cardiomyopathy, typically with later onset and milder course than affected males, its risk rising with age and tracking skewed X-inactivation - which is why carriers warrant their own cardiac surveillance.

edges/1.description: Abolishing the muscle isoform sets up a tissue-specific failure of compensation that is resolved at the next node.

edges/2.description: Loss of dystrophin removes the core structural component of the DGC at the cardiomyocyte sarcolemma.

edges/3.description: A DGC-deficient sarcolemma cannot withstand the mechanical stress of contraction.

edges/4.description: Membrane microdamage admits pathological calcium influx into the cardiomyocyte.

edges/5.description: Sarcolemmal microtears leak creatine kinase into the circulation, though variably in this cardiac-predominant phenotype.

edges/6.description: Sustained calcium overload triggers cardiomyocyte death and secondary fibrosis.

edges/7.description: Cumulative myocyte loss and fibrotic replacement impair contraction and dilate the ventricle.

edges/11.description: In heterozygous carrier females the same structural endpoint manifests later and more mildly, its expression governed by skewed X-inactivation.

edges/12.description: Myocyte loss and fibrosis create a re-entrant/ectopic arrhythmic substrate.

edges/14.description: A sustained malignant ventricular arrhythmia can precipitate fatal circulatory arrest.

evidence.snippet: XLCM is due to an abnormality within the centromeric half of the dystrophin genomic region in heart.
evidence.explanation: Localizes the causal lesion to the dystrophin (DMD) gene, establishing XLDCM as a dystrophinopathy.

evidence.snippet: Two younger patients diagnosed as having X-linked dilated cardiomyopathy (XLDCM) developed congestive heart failure without overt skeletal myopathy.
evidence.explanation: Documents the exon 45-55 in-frame deletion class producing cardiac-predominant XLDCM without skeletal myopathy.

genes/0.notes: The same gene as Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy. XLDCM arises from a specific subset of DMD lesions that damage cardiac dystrophin while sparing skeletal muscle: (1) deletions of the muscle (M) promoter and first muscle exon at the 5' end, which abolish the muscle isoform (the paradigmatic "5' XLDCM"); (2) in-frame deletions in the exon 45-55 hotspot, which can present cardiac-predominantly with mild or absent skeletal disease; and (3) destabilizing missense variants. The functional consequence is loss or destabilization of dystrophin rather than a gain-of-function or dominant-negative effect.

evidence.snippet: While some patients may have benefited from 'early' (active) as opposed to 'delayed' (placebo) initiation of perindopril and bisoprolol, group-mean ventricular function did not differ between study arms after 60 months.
evidence.explanation: The prophylaxis-versus-treat-at-detection nuance that qualifies how this therapy is timed.

treatments/0.description: Standard heart-failure guideline-directed medical therapy is the mainstay for the dilated cardiomyopathy: an ACE inhibitor, usually combined with a beta-blocker. Combination therapy improved left ventricular function relative to ACE-inhibitor monotherapy in the dystrophinopathy-cardiomyopathy literature. An important recent caveat from the DMD Heart Protection Study long-term follow-up is that starting therapy prophylactically (before detectable dysfunction) did not produce a group-mean ejection-fraction advantage over starting at first detected dysfunction, though the trial notes small numbers and echo insensitivity - so early detection and prompt treatment at first dysfunction is the defensible strategy rather than universal prophylaxis.

evidence.snippet: DMD Care Standards recommend starting angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEi) medication empirically no later than the age of 10 years
evidence.explanation: The standard-of-care recommendation to treat dystrophin-deficient cardiomyopathy with an ACE inhibitor.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Standard neurohormonal-blockade heart-failure therapy acting on the ventricular remodeling and failure endpoint rather than on the dystrophin deficit.

evidence.snippet: There is no therapeutic difference in EF improvement between lisinopril and losartan over the one-year duration for treatment of boys with DMD-related CM.
evidence.explanation: The randomized trial establishing losartan (ARB) as equivalent to lisinopril (ACE inhibitor) for dystrophin-deficient cardiomyopathy, supporting the ARB as an alternative.

treatments/1.description: An angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan is an accepted alternative to an ACE inhibitor; a randomized double-blind trial of lisinopril versus losartan in dystrophin-deficient cardiomyopathy found both effective without establishing superiority of either.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Renin-angiotensin blockade as an alternative to ACE inhibition for the failing ventricle.

evidence.snippet: heart transplantation is a safe and effective treatment for selected patients with end-stage DCM.
evidence.explanation: The authors' conclusion supporting transplantation in selected dystrophinopathic DCM patients.

evidence.snippet: cardiac transplantation is offered to persons with severe dilated cardiomyopathy and BMD with limited or no clinical evidence of skeletal muscle disease
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states that transplantation is offered when skeletal muscle disease is limited or absent - precisely the XLDCM situation that makes it a favorable candidate.

treatments/2.description: The only curative option for end-stage dystrophin-deficient heart failure refractory to medical therapy. XLDCM is a favorable transplant setting precisely because skeletal and respiratory function is typically preserved - the comorbidity that complicates transplant candidacy in classic Duchenne is largely absent here - and post-transplant outcomes are comparable to non-dystrophinopathy recipients.

evidence.snippet: Heart transplantation (HT) is the only curative therapy for patients with dystrophinopathic end-stage heart failure who remain symptomatic despite an optimal medical therapy.
evidence.explanation: States transplantation as the only curative option for end-stage dystrophinopathic cardiomyopathy.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Replaces the failing organ rather than acting on the dystrophin deficit, which persists in the remaining tissues.

evidence.snippet: Cardiac symptoms are particularly prevalent in female dystrophin mutation carriers, affecting about 8% of this population with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) as a common presentation
evidence.explanation: The carrier cardiac risk that justifies extending surveillance to heterozygous females.

evidence.snippet: For heterozygous females: cardiac evaluation at least once after the teenage years
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews' explicit surveillance recommendation for heterozygous carrier females.

treatments/3.description: Because subclinical cardiac dysfunction precedes symptoms and skeletal severity does not predict cardiac involvement, baseline and serial cardiac evaluation (ECG, echocardiography, and cardiac MRI for late gadolinium enhancement) is standard from diagnosis in affected individuals. Heterozygous carrier females need surveillance too, given their real, X-inactivation-dependent cardiomyopathy risk.

evidence.snippet: cardiac resynchronization therapy (biventricular pacing), is appropriate for cases of heart failure with associated ventricular dyssynchrony
evidence.explanation: The review's statement of CRT indication in dystrophinopathy cardiomyopathy with ventricular dyssynchrony.

treatments/4.description: For advanced disease, an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator addresses the ventricular arrhythmia / sudden-death risk, and cardiac resynchronization therapy (biventricular pacing) is used when heart failure is complicated by ventricular dyssynchrony.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Device therapy targets the arrhythmic substrate and dyssynchronous failure rather than the dystrophin deficit.

evidence.snippet: Several mouse models have been developed to study molecular and pathological consequences of dystrophin deficiency, but do not recapitulate all aspects of human disease pathology and exhibit a mild cardiac phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Direct evidence that standard mouse models under-represent the human cardiac phenotype, the mismatch this discussion records.

open_questions/0.rationale: The node that makes XLDCM a distinct entity is the ventricle-selective loss of dystrophin driven by failed brain-isoform compensation in the human ventricle. Existing models do not reproduce this selectivity: standard mdx mice show only a mild, late cardiac phenotype; enhanced backgrounds (Cmah-null) and large-animal canine models accelerate or better match the course but carry combined skeletal-plus-cardiac dystrophin loss. The isoform-topography mechanism therefore rests on human autopsy/explant tissue (Neri 2012), and translational validity of model-derived cardiac findings to the cardiac-selective human phenotype remains the open question - so cross-model agreement should be judged mechanism by mechanism rather than treating a mild or combined-phenotype model as representative.

evidence.snippet: The E3 ubiquitin ligase HUWE1 has been implicated in TP53-associated regulation of the neuronal cell cycle.
evidence.explanation: Supports the limited neuronal-cell-cycle role stated in the node without extending it to a complete developmental mechanism.

evidence.snippet: For the other genes, expression array and quantitative PCR analysis in patient cell lines compared to controls showed a significant upregulation of HSD17B10 and HUWE1 as well as several important genes in their molecular pathways.
evidence.explanation: Supports increased HUWE1 expression in the initially reported Xp11.22 duplication cohort; later high-resolution mapping narrowed the minimal region to HUWE1.

evidence.snippet: Taken together, these findings suggest that p. G4310R mutation identified in the affected male from the JMS family (K9149) leads to reduced E3 ligase levels and consequent accumulation of downstream targets p53 and Mcl1.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports reduced HUWE1 abundance and increased substrate abundance for p.G4310R.

evidence.snippet: In family 3, levels of the HUWE1 p.R4063Q protein were increased, and consequently the levels of p53 substrate were reduced in the two affected brothers compared with their normal father (figure 4).
evidence.explanation: Shows the opposite allele-specific direction for HUWE1 and p53 abundance, preventing a uniform loss-of-function claim.

steps/1.description: HUWE1 is a HECT-domain E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase implicated in regulation of the neuronal cell cycle. Xp11.22 duplications can increase HUWE1 expression, while different missense alleles can decrease or increase HUWE1 protein and shift the abundance of its substrates p53 and Mcl-1 in opposite directions. The direct evidence therefore supports allele-specific dysregulation of HUWE1-dependent substrate homeostasis, not a uniform loss or gain of catalytic activity across the allelic spectrum. This abundance/substrate branch is kept distinct from the AMBRA1-RMC1 mitochondrial-recruitment branch because the available evidence does not establish a causal connection between them.

evidence.snippet: The p.G4310R mutation did not affect HUWE1 activity but instead reduced its stability, leading to p53 accumulation and consequently increased expression of p53 target genes.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports reduced HUWE1 stability while distinguishing that defect from loss of HUWE1 activity.

evidence.snippet: In vitro ubiquitination assays indicated that both HECT G4310R and HECT WT ubiquitinate p53 with similar efficiencies (Figure 2B), thus indicating that G4310R does not affect HUWE1 catalytic HECT domain activity.
evidence.explanation: The p.G4310R HECT domain retained wild-type-like p53 ubiquitination efficiency, so abnormal protein ubiquitination is not asserted for this node.

steps/2.description: In Juberg-Marsidi syndrome cells, p.G4310R reduces HUWE1 stability and protein abundance. The mutant HECT domain ubiquitinates p53 with efficiency similar to wild type, so this node represents an allele-specific stability defect rather than impaired catalytic p53 ubiquitination. It must not be generalized to all HUWE1 sequence variants or to regional Xp11.22 copy gains.

evidence.snippet: HUWE1 p.G4310R levels were reduced, and p53 accumulated in JMS LCs (Figure 2A).
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the separate p53 protein-accumulation step in p.G4310R patient-derived cells.

steps/3.description: Reduced p.G4310R HUWE1 abundance is followed by accumulation of p53 protein in patient-derived Juberg-Marsidi syndrome lymphoblastoid cells. This is an allele-specific molecular abundance finding rather than evidence of reduced catalytic p53 ubiquitination by the mutant HECT domain.

evidence.snippet: Mechanistically, AMBRA1 acts as a mitochondrial scaffold that recruits RMC1, enabling HUWE1 localization to mitochondria through direct interaction with RMC1.
evidence.explanation: The zebrafish-centered study supports the AMBRA1 scaffold and RMC1-HUWE1 recruitment route; the node description makes the disease-associated disruption, not normal recruitment, the abnormal state.

steps/4.description: Under normal experimental conditions, AMBRA1 acts as a mitochondrial scaffold for RMC1, and RMC1 directly interacts with HUWE1 to recruit it to mitochondria. Disease-associated noncatalytic variants disrupt this recruitment, so the abnormal state modeled here is failed mitochondrial targeting rather than normal recruitment. This compartment-specific route is not generalized to all HUWE1 substrates or alleles.

evidence.snippet: Global ubiquitin profiling reveals that these variants selectively disrupt the ubiquitination of mitochondrial proteins without affecting nuclear substrates.
evidence.explanation: Supports a selective mitochondrial-substrate ubiquitination defect and explicitly bounds the claim against a global nuclear-substrate defect.

evidence.snippet: Disruption of this recruitment by disease-associated HUWE1 variants prevents mitochondrial targeting and impairs mitochondrial substrate ubiquitination.
evidence.explanation: Links disease-associated variants to failed mitochondrial targeting and substrate ubiquitination in the mechanistic assays.

steps/5.description: Patient-associated noncatalytic HUWE1 variants M375I, G660R, and H669Q disrupt mitochondrial targeting and impair ubiquitination of mitochondrial substrates. The reported profiling did not show an effect on nuclear substrates, so this node represents compartment-selective dysfunction rather than global loss of HUWE1 catalytic activity.

evidence.snippet: By focusing on Juberg-Marsidi syndrome (JMS), one of the severest XLIDs, we show that increased p53 signaling results from p53 accumulation caused by HUWE1 p.G4310R destabilization.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports increased p53 signaling downstream of p53 accumulation caused by p.G4310R HUWE1 destabilization.

steps/6.description: Accumulated p53 is accompanied by increased expression of p53 target genes in p.G4310R Juberg-Marsidi syndrome cells. This signaling state is modeled separately from both HUWE1 protein destabilization and p53 protein accumulation.

evidence.snippet: This further alters cell-cycle progression and proliferation in JMS cells.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports altered cell-cycle progression and proliferation in patient-derived JMS cells.

steps/7.description: Increased p53 signaling in p.G4310R patient-derived lymphoblastoid cells is associated with G1 accumulation, reduced S-phase entry, and reduced proliferation. These are cellular disease-model findings rather than a directly measured patient phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Modeling of JMS neurodevelopment reveals majorly impaired neural differentiation accompanied by increased p53 signaling.
evidence.explanation: Supports impaired neural differentiation and increased p53 signaling in patient-derived hiPSC models.

evidence.snippet: The neural differentiation defects can be successfully rescued by reducing p53 levels and restoring the expression of p53 target genes, in particular CDKN1A/p21.
evidence.explanation: p53-reduction rescue supports a causal p53 contribution to the in-vitro neural-differentiation defect.

steps/8.description: Two hiPSC clones derived from one p.G4310R Juberg-Marsidi patient formed fewer neural rosettes and showed reduced neural maturation markers. p53 knockdown restored rosette formation and neural maturation markers, providing rescue evidence for p53 dependence while remaining an in-vitro, single-patient model.

evidence.snippet: In zebrafish, noncatalytic HUWE1 variants found in XLID patients (M375I, G660R, and H669Q) recapitulate key neurodevelopmental deficits, including impaired brain growth and motor neuron defects.
evidence.explanation: Supports motor-neuron defects specifically in variant-expressing zebrafish.

steps/9.description: In zebrafish, the patient-associated noncatalytic HUWE1 variants M375I, G660R, and H669Q produce motor-neuron defects. This model-organism readout is kept distinct from impaired whole-brain growth and is not direct evidence of a human motor-neuron mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Defects in JMS neurodevelopment were further evident in altered cortical cytoarchitecture, resulting in a disorganized layer of proliferating NPCs and reduced JMS brain organoid size.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the separate cerebral-organoid growth and cortical-architecture readout.

steps/10.description: Cerebral organoids derived from the p.G4310R patient line were smaller and showed altered cortical cytoarchitecture, including a disorganized layer of proliferating neural progenitor cells. This is a distinct organoid-level architecture readout from the hiPSC neural-differentiation assay and remains a single-patient in-vitro model.

evidence.snippet: In zebrafish, noncatalytic HUWE1 variants found in XLID patients (M375I, G660R, and H669Q) recapitulate key neurodevelopmental deficits, including impaired brain growth and motor neuron defects.
evidence.explanation: Supports impaired brain growth specifically in variant-expressing zebrafish.

steps/11.description: In zebrafish, the patient-associated noncatalytic HUWE1 variants M375I, G660R, and H669Q reproduce impaired brain growth. This model-organism readout is kept distinct from the motor-neuron defect and is not represented as direct proof of the corresponding mechanism in patients.

evidence.snippet: All individuals presented with ID (Table 1).
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the 100% frequency assignment within the 21-person clinical cohort.

evidence.snippet: The majority had global developmental delay (20/21).
evidence.explanation: The reported 20/21 frequency maps directly to VERY_FREQUENT.

evidence.snippet: The condition is characterized by variable phenotypes, including global developmental delay, intellectual disability, and distinctive facial dysmorphisms, with inheritance patterns ranging from X-linked recessive to de novo mutations in females.
evidence.explanation: The current case series and literature review independently retains global developmental delay as a characteristic feature.

evidence.snippet: The mean age of walking was 2 ½ years while three patients never achieved autonomous walking (P4, P5 and P16)
evidence.explanation: Directly supports delayed acquisition of walking and failure to achieve autonomous walking in the clinical cohort, specifically anchoring the motor-delay phenotype.

evidence.snippet: In total, 17/19 had speech delay, with absence of speech (or <5 words) in 13/19 patients.
evidence.explanation: The reported 17/19 frequency maps directly to VERY_FREQUENT and supports the severe end of the speech phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Hypotonia was present in 14/20.
evidence.explanation: The reported 14/20 frequency maps directly to FREQUENT.

evidence.snippet: Seizures were reported in 7/18 patients with onset between 9 months and 13 years.
evidence.explanation: The reported 7/18 frequency maps directly to FREQUENT.

evidence.snippet: Postnatal short stature occurred in 70% of patients in the literature, with the same rate in our series (71%).

genes/0.notes: HUWE1 (Xp11.22) encodes a HECT-domain E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase. The original Turner family had macrocephaly and was subsequently associated with a HUWE1 missense variant; it was not one of the Xp11.22 microduplication families. Pathogenic missense and rare splice-site variants underlie the broader syndromic spectrum. Separately, Xp11.22 duplications can increase HUWE1 dosage. Later high-resolution mapping of 12 copy-number gains narrowed the minimal duplicated region to HUWE1 alone and found increased HUWE1, but not HSD17B10, mRNA. Juberg-Marsidi and Brooks (Brooks-Wisniewski-Brown) syndromes were shown to be HUWE1-allelic. M375I, G660R, and H669Q are patient-associated noncatalytic variants examined in the mitochondrial-recruitment study; their experimental mechanism should not be generalized to every pathogenic HUWE1 allele.

open_questions/0.rationale: The clinical sequence-variant cohorts and p.G4310R cellular mechanism should not be pooled with copy-gain cases. Although the original Xp11.22 report described a larger interval, later high-resolution mapping narrowed the minimal duplicated region to HUWE1 and detected increased HUWE1, but not HSD17B10, mRNA. This is an interpretation boundary, not a diagnostic test.

evidence.snippet: We describe for the first time that females can be severely affected, despite preferential inactivation of the affected X chromosome.

open_questions/1.rationale: Severe female disease can occur despite preferential inactivation of the affected X in accessible tissue, whereas inherited male cases can have clinically unaffected carrier mothers. Accessible-tissue XCI therefore cannot yet explain or predict female severity.

open_questions/2.rationale: Alleles can alter HUWE1 abundance, p53/Mcl-1 homeostasis, or mitochondrial recruitment in different directions. The abstract reports three conserved hotspots with clinical impact but does not establish a validated severity classifier.

open_questions/3.rationale: The sanctioned cohort cache does not provide adult natural-history or tumor-risk results. HUWE1 and p53 biology alone does not license a germline cancer-risk claim or syndrome-specific tumor surveillance; longitudinal adult data are needed.

evidence.snippet: Notably, Urolithin A treatment ameliorates neurodevelopmental phenotypes in HUWE1-deficient zebrafish.
evidence.explanation: Documents preclinical rescue in zebrafish only; it does not support clinical treatment or efficacy in humans.

open_questions/4.rationale: The disease-associated mitochondrial-recruitment disruption and Urolithin A rescue were established in a zebrafish-centered model-organism study. No patient tissue or clinical intervention establishes that this branch drives human HNDD or that mitochondrial quality-control enhancement is safe or effective in people. Urolithin A is therefore intentionally excluded from treatments and retained solely as a zebrafish translation gap.
